Four times the data per frame to move and store
Multipath structure narrow captures cannot separate
Results on 56 tones are not automatically results on 996
More antenna × subcarrier dimensions for the covariance
Short windows leave the covariance ill-conditioned

cards.front:
HE — what does it stand for, and what does it give sensing that older PHYs
do not?
cards.title: HE
cards.why:
For sensing the gift is RESOLUTION. Our adapter yields 242 tones per antenna
pair on a 20 MHz channel and 996 at 160 MHz. Most of the CSI literature was
written on 56.

Two things follow. More tones resolve multipath structure narrow captures
cannot separate at all. And the covariance analysis depends on the count of
antenna-by-subcarrier dimensions, so a richer tone grid changes the detection
budget directly — which means results on 56 subcarriers are not automatically
results on 996.

cards.back:
Internet of Things. The useful definition is structural rather than
aspirational: a **network of things** is built from five primitives —

- **sensors** that measure a physical property,
- **aggregators** that turn groups of raw readings into something smaller,
- **communication channels** that move data between sensing, computing and
  acting,
- **eUtilities** — the software or hardware doing the computing, a phone or
  a cloud,
- **decision triggers** — predicates that must be true before an action
  fires.

The field's surveys divide the subject three ways: **things-oriented** (the
sensors), **internet-oriented** (the middleware), and **semantic-oriented**
(making the data mean something). Their point is that IoT is useful only
where all three intersect — sensors without semantics are a data landfill.
cards.example:
The decision trigger is the primitive worth pointing at, because it is the
one people forget is part of the architecture.

Ours is the recalibration rule, and it is literally a predicate: fire a
calibration campaign when the CSI estimate and the device-count reference
have disagreed enough, for long enough, by a margin large enough to matter.
The last clause is a measured addition — a purely statistical version of the
same predicate fired on a third of certified-empty streams at a few
thousandths of a decibel.

Name the five primitives for any building and the same exercise works:
sensors, aggregators, channels, eUtilities, triggers. The argument the thesis
makes with the word is ORDINARINESS — no bespoke hardware, only the five
things a modern building already has.

figures.caption: The five primitives, named for this deployment. The dashed return is what makes it a loop rather than a pipeline: the trigger decides when the sensors get re-anchored.

cards.front:
IoT — give a definition with actual content, and name the parts such a
system has to have.
cards.title: IoT
cards.why:
Our deployment is one of these, part for part, and saying so precisely
beats gesturing at the word. The nodes are sensors. The capture service is
the aggregator. The tailnet is the communication channel. S3 and the
measurement lake are eUtilities. And the recalibration rule is **literally a
decision trigger** — a predicate that must hold before a campaign fires.

So the argument the thesis makes with this word is one of ORDINARINESS: the
architecture needs no bespoke hardware, only the five primitives a modern
building already has.

cards.back:
Integrated Sensing and Communication: designing one waveform, one radio and
one slice of spectrum to carry data AND perform radar-like sensing, rather
than building two systems.

The clean way to state the cost is as a frontier. For a fixed waveform,
bandwidth and power budget, the achievable pairs of (data rate, sensing
accuracy) form a boundary. You can sit anywhere on it. You cannot sit
outside it, and a waveform optimised for one end is measurably worse at the
other.
cards.example:
Our own preamble is the worked case. CSI comes from the training symbols at
the start of a frame, and those symbols exist to let the receiver equalise
the channel — a communication job. Their number, spacing and duration were
chosen for that job.

So the sensing resolution available to us is whatever those symbols happen
to provide: 242 tones on a 20 MHz channel, once per frame, at whatever rate
the traffic happens to be. A radar designed for the same room would choose a
waveform for delay resolution instead and do better on every sensing metric.

This is why "use a bigger network" is not an answer to a sensing accuracy
question, and why the honest framing of the deployment case is cost and
ubiquity rather than performance.

figures.caption: The shape of the trade-off, illustrative rather than measured. A communication-first system sits at the left-hand end: nearly all the rate, whatever sensing falls out of the preamble. Sensing fidelity from commodity WiFi is therefore bounded by a design decision made before we arrived.
figures.x_label: share of the waveform budget spent on sensing

cards.front: ISAC — what is the idea, and what does it cost?
cards.title: ISAC
cards.why:
It matters twice, in opposite directions.

Optimistically: it is the standardisation horizon. If access points ship
sensing as a first-class network service, CSI sensing stops being a
commodity-hardware exploit dependent on driver patches.

Pessimistically, and more usefully: ISAC theory proves a TRADE-OFF. One
waveform serving two purposes cannot maximise both — sensing accuracy is paid
for in communication rate. Operating in a band whose primary obligation is
communication, we inherit a bounded sensing budget. Attainable fidelity is
principled and finite, not something a better estimator lifts without limit.

cards.back:
Leave-One-Environment-Out: hold out an ENTIRE environment, train on the rest,
test on the one held out, and repeat for each. The score reported is the
average over folds, and every fold's test set is a room the model has never
seen.
cards.example:
The two protocols on the same corpus, and why the gap between them is the
finding rather than a nuisance.

Under a random 80/20 split, windows from every room appear in both halves.
A per-link amplitude map scores well, because at test time it is recognising
rooms it memorised. Under LOEO, the same feature on the same corpus
collapses — its R² can go negative, which means it does worse than guessing
the average.

Neither number is wrong. They answer different questions, and only the
second one is the question a deployment asks. The reason this thesis reports
LOEO for every transfer claim is that the first number is not merely
optimistic — it is measuring memorisation.

figures.caption: The difference is where the fold boundary is drawn. A random split cuts through every room, so each room appears on both sides; LOEO cuts between rooms, so the test room is genuinely unseen.

cards.front:
LOEO — what is the protocol, and what question does it answer that a random
split cannot?
cards.title: LOEO
cards.why:
A random split lets windows from the same room land on both sides. The model
then learns that room's multipath fingerprint and scores brilliantly on data
it has effectively already seen. The number is real and answers the wrong
question.

Everyday version: revising with the exam paper in front of you. Your mark
says nothing about whether you could sit a different paper.

LOEO is the only honest way to ask "would this work in a building we have
never been in?", and it is the protocol behind the headline calibration
result — where two labelled anchors in the new environment recover most of
the transfer loss.

cards.back:
Line of Sight: an unobstructed straight path from transmitter to receiver.
Where one exists it usually dominates the received energy, because every
other path is longer and has bounced off something lossy.
cards.example:
The same person, two rooms, two different measurements — and it is the
geometry that decides which.

**Corridor, clean line of sight.** The direct path carries most of the
energy. A body standing in it removes a large share, so the MEAN amplitude
drops visibly and the variance moves less. Blockage regime.

**Furnished reading room, shelving between the nodes.** There is no dominant
path to block. The body perturbs many comparable paths at once, so the mean
barely moves and the SPREAD rises. Variance regime.

A pipeline that carried only one of the two feature families would work in
one of those rooms and fail in the other, with no error message. That is why
both are kept and why the crossover between them is band-dependent rather
than a constant.

figures.caption: Two geometries, two different features. Which one carries the count is decided by whether there is a dominant direct path to shadow.

nodes.label: strong LOS — the body BLOCKS: mean amplitude falls
no strong LOS — the body STIRS: spread rises

cards.front: LOS — what is it, and which counting feature does its presence decide?
cards.title: LOS
cards.why:
It decides WHICH amplitude feature carries the count — a real design
consequence rather than a definition.

With a strong direct path, a body standing in it blocks a large share of the
energy, so the MEAN amplitude drops: shadowing. With no strong direct path
the channel is already a diffuse mixture, and an extra body mostly stirs the
mixture, so the SPREAD rises: variance.

Two geometrically distinct mechanisms, competing rather than combining, which
is why a practical pipeline keeps both feature families and why the crossover
between them is band-dependent.

cards.back:
Leave-One-Subject-Out: hold out an entire PERSON, so the model is tested on
someone it never trained on. The same discipline as LOEO applied to identity
rather than place.
cards.example:
The protocol as the activity-recognition literature runs it: nineteen
activities performed by eight subjects, with seven subjects' feature vectors
used for training and the eighth held out, repeated eight times and averaged.
The argument its authors give is exactly the LOEO argument moved one axis
over — treating subjects as UNITS, so no trial from the same person appears
on both sides.

Why it is not our axis, stated as a limitation rather than a boast: our
target is a COUNT of anonymous bodies. Body diversity certainly affects the
signal — the generalisability survey ranks human body diversity as one of
three primary factors, alongside device heterogeneity and environment. We do
not control it and we claim nothing about it, which is the honest position
for a study whose participants were not sampled for physique.

figures.caption: Three ways to cut a corpus, and the question each answers. The last column says which of them this thesis actually reports.
rows: does the model fit this corpus?
**would it work in a new building?**
would it work on another radio?
would it work on a new body?
no — not an axis we control

cards.front: LOSO — what is held out, and is it one of our axes?
cards.title: LOSO
cards.why:
Standard in activity recognition, where body size and gait differ enough to
be a domain shift in their own right.

NOT one of our axes. This thesis shifts on environment and on hardware, and
it counts anonymous bodies rather than recognising named ones — so subject
identity is neither a variable we control nor one we claim robustness to.

cards.back:
Medium Access Control: the layer deciding WHO TRANSMITS WHEN on a shared
medium. In 802.11 the fundamental method is CSMA/CA — a station wanting to
transmit may do so only after listening and finding the channel idle. If it
is busy, the station waits for it to clear and then waits an additional
random **backoff interval**, so that two waiting stations do not collide the
instant it frees up. The receiver acknowledges a good frame; no
acknowledgement means resend.

There is a clever shortcut: every frame announces its own length, so a
listening station can note how long the channel will be occupied and stop
physically sensing until then. That is virtual carrier sense.

"MAC address" is a separate meaning: the hardware identifier a device puts in
every frame it sends.
cards.example:
How the protocol becomes an occupancy signal, on our own instrument.

Our illuminator emits frames at a commanded rate. Under CSMA/CA it must find
the channel idle first, so as the room fills with active devices it defers
more often and lands fewer frames. The delivered fraction therefore falls as
device activity rises — and the rate ladder showed exactly that: delivery
tracks competing channel load rather than commanded rate.

So a quantity that looks like a nuisance is a second, free occupancy channel,
already recorded in every capture ever taken.

The address half has the opposite sign. Phones randomise their MAC precisely
so they cannot be tracked, so one phone can present several identifiers in an
hour. Counting identifiers overcounts devices, before you reach the harder
question of devices versus people.

figures.caption: Listen, wait, wait a random extra interval, then speak. More devices in the room means more waiting — which is why our delivery deficit is an occupancy signal rather than a nuisance.

nodes.label: the random wait is what stops two waiting stations colliding

cards.front:
MAC — what does the layer actually do, and how does that become an occupancy
signal?
cards.title: MAC
cards.why:
Both halves are load-bearing, in different chapters.

The protocol half gives us a count channel for free. More active devices
means more competing traffic, which means our paced probe defers more often
and lands less reliably. That delivery deficit rises with activity — an
occupancy signal already recorded in every capture ever taken.

The address half is the privacy floor. Phones randomise their MAC address
precisely so they cannot be tracked, so one phone can appear as several
identifiers. Counting identifiers overcounts devices — before you even reach
the harder question of devices versus people.

cards.example:
Two models on the same five windows, chosen so that average error cannot
tell them apart.

Model A misses by 2, 2, 2, 2, 2 — MAE **2.0**. Model B misses by
0, 0, 0, 0, 10 — MAE also **2.0**. Identical on this metric. For a
ventilation controller, A is a mild nuisance and B is four correct answers
and one evacuation-scale error.

Now the version that actually happened in this thesis. The point contract
and the distributional contract score nearly the same MAE under environment
shift, and separate sharply on band-level scoring and on calibration. A
results table with one metric column would have shown two equivalent
systems, and the conclusion would have been that the contract does not
matter.
cards.explanation:
Mean Absolute Error: average the size of each mistake, ignoring direction.
In our units it reads directly — "on average, off by about one person" —
which is why the literature uses it and why comparison needs it.

Two properties are worth knowing. It is in the SAME UNITS as the thing being
predicted, so it needs no interpretation. And it treats all mistakes in
proportion, so it is dominated by the many typical cases rather than by the
few bad ones.

It is refused as the ONLY metric for an empirical reason rather than a
stylistic one. Scored on average error alone, the point and distributional
output contracts are nearly indistinguishable under environment shift.
Scored on where they place their probability mass, and on whether their
stated confidence stays honest, they are not remotely so — and it is the
second pair that predicts whether a deployment moved to a new room can be
trusted.

Reporting only average error would have concealed the single clearest
cross-environment result the thesis holds. That is the argument, and it is
worth being able to make.

fields.meaning: the true count for window i
what the model predicted for it
absolute value — a miss of −2 and a miss of +2 cost the same
number of windows scored

figures.caption: What choosing a metric means. Under MAE, being out by six costs exactly three times what being out by two costs. Under a squared metric it costs nine times as much. Neither is more correct — they encode different answers to "how much worse is one big mistake than several small ones?".

curves.label: MAE: cost grows with the size of the miss
RMSE's inner term: cost grows with its square

cards.question:
MAE — what is it exactly, and why does this thesis refuse to report it
alone?
cards.reading:
Add up the sizes of all the mistakes, ignoring their direction, and divide
by how many there were.
cards.title: MAE

cards.back:
Multiple-Input Multiple-Output: several antennas at each end, so several
spatially distinct copies of the channel exist at once. In communication it
buys throughput and robustness; in sensing it buys VIEWPOINTS.

Plain version. One antenna at each end gives you one path through the room —
one opinion about what is in it. Two at each end gives you four, because
every transmit antenna reaches every receive antenna, and each of those four
paths bounces off the furniture differently. Nothing about the room changed;
the number of independent looks at it did.

What it changes about a record is its SHAPE. A single-antenna record is a
vector over subcarriers. A 2 × 2 record is a matrix per subcarrier, so the
whole frame is an order-3 block of complex numbers.
cards.example:
Two generations of hardware, same idea, different sizes — and the arithmetic
is worth doing because it is where the corpus's numbers come from.

The **Intel 5300**, which most of the published CSI literature runs on,
reports 30 subcarriers per antenna pair on a 20 MHz channel. With 3 × 3
antennas that is 30 matrices of 3 × 3 per record, or 270 complex numbers.

Our **AX210** node reports 242 tones on the same 20 MHz channel with 2 × 2
antennas: 242 matrices of 2 × 2, or 968 complex numbers per record — and
996 tones at 160 MHz. Roughly a factor of four more dimensions per frame,
from hardware bought in a shop.

The sting is in the last sentence of the "why". Those 968 dimensions are the
p in the detection-edge ratio γ = p/n, so more antennas and more tones RAISE
the number of snapshots needed before an occupant's eigenvalue clears the
noise. More looks at the room is not automatically more counting power.

figures.caption: A 2 × 2 link is four channels, not one. Each transmit antenna reaches each receive antenna by its own set of bounces, so a body that barely disturbs one path can dominate another.

nodes.label: 4 channels × 242 tones = 968 complex numbers per frame

figures.caption: The same record, three ways of counting it. The right-hand column is what feeds the detection edge — which is why a bigger record is not automatically a better one.

cards.front:
MIMO — what is it in plain words, and what does it change about a CSI
record?
cards.title: MIMO
cards.why:
Two practical consequences. The CSI-ratio trick exists only because two
antennas share one radio chain and therefore share its oscillator errors
exactly. And the covariance analysis counts antenna-by-subcarrier dimensions
as one number, so antennas and subcarriers trade against each other in
setting how many occupants are detectable at all.

cards.back:
Network Interface Card: the radio itself — chipset, firmware, antennas, and
the driver exposing them. For sensing purposes a NIC is best classified not
by brand but by **how you get CSI out of it**, because that is what decides
what your data looks like and who else can reproduce it.

Four families, and they are not interchangeable:

- **Intel 5300** with the Linux 802.11n CSI Tool — 30 subcarriers per
  antenna pair, 802.11n only. The platform most of the published corpus
  runs on.
- **Atheros** with the Atheros CSI Tool — 56 subcarriers, a different
  subcarrier layout and a different scaling convention.
- **Broadcom / Cypress** via Nexmon — patched firmware on phones and
  embedded chips; wide coverage, and no vendor support.
- **Intel AX210** via a patched driver — 802.11ax, 242 tones at 20 MHz and
  996 at 160 MHz. What our nodes use.

ESP32-class chips are a fifth case: CSI is a documented API rather than an
exploit, at far lower resolution.
cards.example:
The field has measured this twice, in two different ways, and both are worth
quoting because they are not our own data.

A public CSI dataset recorded the same activities with **Netgear** and with
**Asus** routers specifically so that transmission-hardware robustness could
be studied; its authors report that the hardware domain change deserves
attention in its own right. And a reproducibility-protocol paper states the
problem in the strongest form: models trained on one device, such as the
Intel 5300, suffer severe degradation or need redesign when moved to
another, such as an Atheros card — partly because vendors lay out their
subcarriers differently and each carries its own hardware-specific
imperfections.

Read the last clause carefully, because it is the whole finding. The
subcarrier LAYOUT differs. So a model trained on one card is partly a model
of that card's tone grid, and no amount of retraining on the same data will
tell you that.

figures.caption: The CSI-capable families as a sensing pipeline sees them. The two right-hand columns are why a dataset is bound to the card that produced it, and why the standardisation route matters.

cards.front:
NIC — what is it, how do the CSI-capable ones differ, and why is a piece of
hardware terminology one of this thesis's central findings?
cards.title: NIC
cards.why:
Because swapping it breaks a trained counter MORE than swapping the room
does, and that ordering was not the expected one.

The mechanism: every environment shows the same RANK relation — more people,
more variability — so presence detection transfers cold. But two hardware
platforms sit in cleanly separated variability bands, so the ABSOLUTE mapping
from signal to count is device-specific. Hold the platform and change the
room: small penalty. Hold the room and change the platform: a penalty of a
couple of persons.

This is the empirical reason calibration must be per DEVICE, not merely per
room, and why the thesis says hardware independence stops at the feature
interface.

cards.back:
Non-Line of Sight: no unobstructed path, so everything arriving has bounced,
diffracted, or passed through something. Every arriving copy has therefore
travelled FURTHER than the straight line, and that single fact explains both
verdicts below.
cards.example:
Two measured statements, from opposite sides of the same wall.

**Ranging.** A fusion-positioning survey reports an NLOS identification and
mitigation method in a real office environment reducing the root-mean-square
absolute range error from **1.3 m to 0.651 m**. Note what that means: the
best available correction still leaves two-thirds of a metre, and the
uncorrected error is metre-scale. That is why this thesis treats BLE RSSI as
a zone BRACKET and never as a range.

**Sensing.** The same room is where the amplitude-variability feature works
best, because there is no dominant path for a body to shadow — so an extra
body stirs many comparable paths at once and the spread rises. A corridor
with a clean line of sight gives better ranging and a WORSE variance signal.

The everyday version: shouting down a corridor tells you where someone is;
the echo in a furnished room tells you the room is full. Same sound, two
different questions, and the good room for one is the bad room for the other.

figures.caption: One physical situation, two tasks, opposite verdicts. The middle column is the mechanism, and it is the same mechanism in both rows.
rows: every path is longer than the straight line — a BIAS, not noise
**many comparable paths, so one body perturbs many at once**
**better; this is the variance feature's home**

figures.caption: Why the bias has a sign. The bounced path is geometrically longer, so a delay-derived distance always reads too far — and averaging more measurements does not remove an error that is one-sided.

nodes.label: delay says: further than the truth

cards.front: NLOS — what is it, and why is it not simply "worse"?
cards.title: NLOS
cards.why:
For RANGING it is unambiguously worse, and the mechanism is geometric rather
than statistical: every extra bounce adds path length, so a distance inferred
from delay reads too far and an angle inferred from a bounced wavefront
points at the wall rather than at the transmitter. The positioning literature
calls this the NLOS bias, and it is a bias — it does not average out.

For device-free SENSING it is not a defect but a regime. A diffuse channel is
a mixture of many comparable paths, so a body perturbs many at once — and the
variability feature does well precisely there.

Same physics, opposite verdicts, which is one reason the two modalities in
this thesis fail in disjoint ways.

cards.back:
Node–Relation Graph: IndoorGML's dual-space view of a building. Primal space
is the rooms themselves; the dual is a graph with a node per room and an edge
wherever two rooms connect. It is what routing runs on.

The construction is a single rule, **Poincaré duality**: a k-dimensional
object in an N-dimensional space maps to an (N − k)-dimensional object in the
dual. So in a 3-D building a 3-D room becomes a 0-dimensional NODE, and the
2-D surface shared by two rooms becomes a 1-dimensional EDGE. Nothing is
chosen; the graph is determined by the geometry.

Two graphs come out of that, and the difference matters. The **adjacency**
graph has an edge for every shared boundary, walls included. The
**connectivity** graph keeps only the navigable ones — the doors — and it is
the connectivity graph that routing uses.
cards.example:
Take our own floor. Two reading rooms sharing a wall with no door between
them are ADJACENT and not CONNECTED: one edge in the adjacency graph, none
in the connectivity graph. A person walking from one to the other must go
through the corridor, which is two edges.

Now the finding. It is tempting to expect the second room to be easy to
sense from the first, because they are adjacent — and radio does pass through
that wall. It is equally tempting to expect a corridor-heavy floor to be
hard, because its graph is long and thin. Neither expectation survived.

What survived was blunter: receiver DENSITY and placement. Once you control
for floor area and receiver count, adjacency structure carries no additional
signal about recoverability. The graph is the right description of the
building and the wrong predictor of the measurement — which is why the
hypothesis was superseded rather than deleted. The question, what makes a
floor hard to sense, is still open.

figures.caption: Primal to dual, by Poincaré duality. Each room becomes a node; each shared boundary becomes an edge. Solid edges are doors and belong to the connectivity graph; the dashed one is a shared wall — adjacency only.
What the graph is good for, and what it turned out not to predict. The last row is the superseded hypothesis, kept because the question is still open.
rows: Can a person walk from here to there, and how far?
yes — this is what it is for
Which rooms share a wall radio can pass through?
**no — the signal was floor area and receiver count**

cards.front:
NRG — what is it, how is it constructed, and what did we learn it does NOT
predict?
cards.title: NRG
cards.why:
It is a natural thing to reach for when asking what makes a floor easy or
hard to sense — and this thesis tested that and found it does NOT.

Room adjacency correlates with coverage only through what it travels with:
floor area, and how many receivers were placed. Hold those fixed and the
topology signal disappears. What drives recoverability is receiver DENSITY
and placement.

The hypothesis was superseded rather than merely refuted: the question
survived, the variable was wrong.

cards.example:
The two numbers that make OFDM concrete, and each carries a consequence.

**312.5 kHz** subcarrier spacing means a 3.2 µs symbol, and 802.11 adds a
guard interval — 0.8 µs in the common case — for 4 µs per symbol. That guard
covers 0.8 µs × 0.3 m/ns = **240 metres** of path-length difference, which is
why indoor echoes never leak into the next symbol and why the channel can be
treated as one complex number per subcarrier at all.

And the tone grid is not a ruler. On a 20 MHz HE channel our adapter reports
242 tones, but the centre subcarrier is nulled and several are pilots — so
subcarrier index does not map linearly onto megahertz, and a plot that
pretends otherwise is lying about where the energy was.
cards.explanation:
Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiplexing. Rather than send one fast stream
over a wide channel, split the channel into many narrow subchannels and send
many slow streams in parallel.

Why bother: a wide fast signal meets a channel that treats different
frequencies differently, and untangling that is hard. Each narrow subchannel
is small enough that the channel looks FLAT across it — one complex number
describes it completely, so equalisation becomes a division rather than a
deconvolution.

"Orthogonal" is the trick that makes it cheap. Subcarriers are spaced so that
each one's spectrum is exactly zero at every other one's centre: they overlap
heavily and still do not interfere. In practice it is an inverse FFT at the
transmitter and an FFT at the receiver, with a guard interval between symbols
so echoes of the previous symbol die out first.

Two consequences for us. Those per-subchannel complex numbers ARE the CSI —
no OFDM, no CSI. And the tone axis is a grid, not a ruler: some subcarriers
are pilots and the centre one is nulled, so subcarrier index does not map
linearly onto frequency, and a plot that pretends otherwise is lying.

fields.meaning: subcarrier spacing — 312.5 kHz in most WiFi
which subcarrier
that subcarrier's spectrum

figures.caption: The spectra overlap heavily — and at the exact centre of each subcarrier every other one is precisely zero. That is orthogonality: packed tight and still separable.

markers.label: every neighbour is zero at each centre

figures.x_label: frequency, in units of subcarrier spacing

cards.question: What does OFDM do, and what does "orthogonal" actually mean here?
cards.reading:
Each subcarrier's spectrum is a sinc centred on its own frequency, and its
zeros land exactly on every other subcarrier's centre.
cards.title: OFDM

cards.back:
Physical Layer: where bits become radio. Four jobs, and CSI is a by-product
of the fourth.

**Modulation** — turn bits into constellation points. BPSK carries one bit
per symbol, QPSK two, 16-QAM four, up to 1024-QAM in 802.11ax at ten. Higher
orders pack the points closer together, so they need a cleaner channel.
**Coding** — add redundancy so a few wrong bits are recoverable. Modulation
and coding are chosen together as an MCS index.
**Timing** — find where the frame starts and where each symbol boundary is,
using the preamble; insert a guard interval between symbols so that echoes of
the previous symbol die out before the next is sampled.
**Channel estimation** — compare the known preamble symbols against what
arrived, per subcarrier. That comparison IS the CSI.

Where the standard stops: 802.11 standardises only the two lowest layers,
physical and data link. Everything above is common to all IEEE LANs and does
not know whether the medium is wireless.
cards.example:
The vendor boundary is visible in one number on a real node, and you can
read it without any special tooling.

A Linux network interface exposes its ARP hardware type as an integer. On
node monad05 the management interface `wlan0` and the AX210's own `wlp1s0`
both report **1** — the Ethernet type, meaning the kernel hands you frames
the way the network stack wants them, with the PHY's own metadata already
stripped. The capture interface `wlp1s0mon0` reports **803**, which is
`ARPHRD_IEEE80211_RADIOTAP`: every frame arrives with a radiotap header
carrying rate, channel, signal and antenna information.

That single digit is the boundary the thesis lives on. Type 1 is the network.
Type 803 is the PHY, talking. And CSI itself is not even in radiotap — it
needs the patched driver, which is one more step past the boundary that a
standard kernel will show you.

figures.caption: Everything above the link layer is the same whether the medium is radio or copper. CSI exists only at the bottom — and whether you may read it is a decision the chipset vendor makes, not the standard.
The vendor boundary, read off a real node. Type 1 means the kernel is handing you network frames; type 803 means it is handing you the PHY's own view. Output from node monad05, 2026-08-26.

steps.note: Onboard Broadcom radio, management plane — Ethernet-framed, no PHY metadata.
The AX210 itself, in station mode. Same answer: still just a network card.
ARPHRD_IEEE80211_RADIOTAP — the monitor interface. Now every frame carries rate, channel, signal and antenna.

figures.caption: One frame through the PHY, in order. The channel estimate is computed at step three because the frame cannot be decoded without it — and is normally thrown away at step five.

messages.label: known preamble vs received → Ĥ(k) per subcarrier
bytes up; Ĥ(k) discarded unless the driver exposes it

cards.front:
PHY — what does it actually DO, where does 802.11 stop, and what does the
vendor control?
cards.title: PHY
cards.why:
It is where our observable is born and where somebody else decides whether we
may read it. CSI is computed in the PHY as a normal step of demodulation and
then usually discarded; getting at it needs patched firmware or a driver that
chooses to expose it.

That is a structural limitation of the modality, not a local inconvenience:
modern chipsets increasingly restrict raw CSI access, narrowing the hardware
anyone can build on. The 802.11bf amendment is the field's answer —
standardise the measurement so it stops depending on vendor goodwill.

cards.back:
Physics-Informed Neural Network: train on data as usual, but add a second
loss term penalising violation of a known physical law. The network is
rewarded for predictions that fit the data AND obey the physics.

The construction is two losses and one knob. The **data loss** is the usual
error at the points you measured. The **physics loss** is evaluated at
points where you measured NOTHING — you substitute the network's own output
into the governing equation and penalise how far from zero the result is,
using automatic differentiation to get the derivatives. A weight decides how
much each term counts.

That second term is the entire appeal: it is supervision at places you never
observed, and it costs no labels.
cards.example:
Why it works on a motorway and not in a reading room — one sentence, and it
is about the data rather than about the method.

On a motorway, traffic is DIRECTED. Density and speed are strongly coupled,
the flow is essentially one-dimensional, and the conservation law therefore
carries real information at every unobserved point: cars entering a stretch
must leave it. Physics-informed traffic estimation earns its keep exactly
there.

In an indoor reading room the velocity field is nearly unobservable —
people move in every direction and stand still for long stretches, so the
mean velocity over a patch is close to zero and its divergence is noise. The
conservation term is then being evaluated on a quantity with no signal in it,
so it constrains nothing, which is precisely what the ablation measured: the
ANTI-physical version performed identically, because none of the three
versions was doing anything.

The general lesson is worth more than the negative: a physics prior is only
as informative as the state variable it constrains is observable.

figures.caption: The construction. The physics loss is evaluated where nothing was measured, which is where its supervision comes from — and also why an unobservable state variable makes it inert.
The ablation that retired it. Four variants, one conclusion: the term's contribution did not depend on the term being correct — so it was not acting as physics.
rows: a law with the physics removed

cards.front: PINN — what is the construction, and what happened when we tried it?
cards.title: PINN
cards.why:
The appeal is obvious where labels are scarce: physics is free supervision,
and it demonstrably works in traffic-state estimation, where the conservation
law is the constraint and sparse probe vehicles are the data.

We tested it on indoor crowd density with the mass-conservation law and it
FAILED — in a way more informative than a plain null. Swapping the physics
for a constant version, then for an ANTI-PHYSICAL version, changed the result
not at all, while plain smoothing with no conservation content beat every
variant. A term whose benefit survives inverting the law it encodes is not
acting as physics.

Reported as a documented negative, because the idea is attractive enough that
it will be proposed again and the evidence retiring it is exactly
reproducible.

cards.example:
Read the table above as the two deployments it describes.

With window 5 included: MAE 2.00, RMSE 2.90, ratio 1.45 — the ratio is
telling you that one case is carrying the error. Remove that window's
outlier, so the errors are 0, 1, 1, 2, 2: MAE falls to **1.20** and RMSE to
**1.41**, a ratio of 1.18. MAE improved by 40%; RMSE improved by 51%.

A team reporting only MAE would describe the outlier as a modest problem. A
team reporting both would notice that most of their squared error is one
window — which is a debugging lead, because a single bad window usually has
a cause: a gain step, a dead receiver, a clock seam.
cards.explanation:
Root-Mean-Square Error: square each mistake, average, take the root. The
squaring punishes large mistakes disproportionately, so it is dominated by
the worst cases in a way average absolute error is not. The root at the end
is cosmetic but useful — it brings the number back into persons, so it can
be compared with MAE directly.

Two facts are worth having cold. RMSE is **always at least as large as MAE**,
with equality only when every error has the same magnitude. And the ratio
between them is a diagnostic: close to 1 means errors are uniform, much
larger than 1 means a few cases dominate. That ratio is often more
informative than either number alone.

Choosing between them states what you fear. If being badly wrong
occasionally is much worse than being slightly wrong often — an evacuation
estimate, say — the squared metric matches your preference. If all mistakes
cost in proportion, average absolute error does.

Where it appears here: the density-estimation ablation that retired the
physics prior. The matched, constant and anti-physical closures landed on
the same high-density value, and that is the observation which settled it.

fields.meaning: the squared miss — this is where large errors gain their weight
the root, which returns the answer to the units of the count
number of windows scored
always true; they are equal only when every error is the same size

figures.caption: A worked sample dataset. Five predictions, one of them badly wrong, and the arithmetic done in full. Drop the outlier and MAE falls by a third while RMSE more than halves — which is the whole difference between the two metrics, on five numbers.

The same five windows with the worst error swept from 0 upwards. MAE rises like a straight line; RMSE bends upward, because one large miss enters as its square. Choosing between them is choosing which of these two lines you want a deployment to be judged by.
figures.x_label: size of the single worst error (persons)

cards.question:
RMSE — state it, and show on a sample dataset how it differs from MAE in
practice.
cards.reading:
Square every mistake, average the squares, then take the square root — and
the result can never be smaller than the mean absolute error.
cards.title: RMSE

cards.example:
Where it earns its place here, with the design that makes the result hard to
attack.

Under environment shift the point contract degrades markedly on band RPS
while the distributional contract does not move at all — with feature,
corpus and splits held fixed so that ONLY the contract varies. That last
clause is the part to say out loud: nobody can reply that the distributional
model was simply a better model, because it is the same model with a
different output.

And the reason this matters operationally: both contracts scored nearly the
same MAE. A results table with average error alone would have shown two
equivalent systems.
cards.explanation:
Ranked Probability Score: scores a whole predicted DISTRIBUTION over ordered
categories, rewarding probability mass placed near the truth. Because the
bands are ordered, being one band out is penalised less than being three out
— which plain classification accuracy cannot express at all.

The mechanism is the cumulative sum. Turn both the forecast and the outcome
into running totals across the bands, then measure how far apart those two
staircases are, squared, band by band. A forecast that puts its mass next
door to the truth has running totals that diverge for one step; a forecast
three bands out diverges for three. Lower is better, and zero means all the
mass sat on the band that happened.

Everyday version: forecasting tomorrow's temperature band. Guessing 15–20 °C
when it is 21 °C is a near miss; guessing 0–5 °C is not. Accuracy calls both
simply wrong.

One honesty note. The vault corpus holds no text on the ranked probability
score itself — the statistics books here cover hypothesis testing,
confidence intervals and regression, and the uncertainty literature here is
conformal rather than scoring-rule based. The definition above is the
standard one from the forecast-verification literature, and it is cited to
nothing in the corpus because there is nothing in the corpus to cite.

fields.meaning: probability the forecast put on band j
1 for the band that happened, 0 for the others
number of ordered bands
the running total up to band k — the cumulative step that encodes ORDER

figures.caption: Three forecasts of the same outcome, worked in full. Truth is band 3. All three put their peak on ONE band, so plain accuracy calls A right and B and C equally wrong — and RPS ranks B far above C, because B was one band out and C was two.
rows: A right; B and C both simply wrong

figures.caption: The shape of the difference. Accuracy is a step: right, or wrong, with nothing in between. RPS keeps growing, so a near miss is scored as a near miss — which is the only way to compare two systems that are both usually close.

curves.label: accuracy — one step and then flat

figures.x_label: how many bands the forecast's mass sits away from the truth

cards.question: RPS — what does it score that accuracy cannot, and how is it computed?
cards.reading:
Add up the squared gaps between the forecast's running total and the
outcome's running total, band by band, and divide by one less than the
number of bands.
cards.title: RPS

cards.example:
Invert the model and watch it fail, with the numbers the positioning
literature reports.

Suppose the reference is −40 dBm at one metre and the environment has
n = 3.5. A phone measured at **−70 dBm** solves to about 7.2 m. Now let the
fading term take its measured indoor magnitude: multipath and body
shadowing routinely move RSSI by more than **10 dB** over a small
displacement, and a body absorbs several more depending on which pocket the
phone is in. At n = 3.5, ten decibels is a factor of about **1.9 in
distance** — so the same measurement is consistent with anywhere between
roughly 4 m and 14 m.

That is why the thesis asks RSSI a question it can answer — "is this
advertiser in this zone?" — and not one it cannot: "how far away is it?".
cards.explanation:
Received Signal Strength Indicator: one number per received frame, the total
power that arrived. No frequency detail, no phase, no per-path structure —
the channel-response curve collapsed to its average.

**Who computes it, and when.** The receiver's own front end, during reception
of the frame's preamble, while the automatic gain control settles. It is
reported per frame as a MAC-layer quantity, which is why any driver can hand
it to you with no patching at all. Its scale is NOT physical: the standard
allows a vendor-defined range up to 255 steps and vendors have historically
chosen differently — one uses 0–100, another 0–60 — so a raw RSSI number is
only comparable against itself on the same hardware.

Both verdicts are true at once, and holding both is the point.

**Too coarse** for body-scale sensing: a person changes WHICH frequencies
fade, and averaging is exactly the operation that erases that. This is the
one-sentence case for CSI.

**Good enough** as a zone anchor: for BLE we only need to know roughly how
far an advertiser is, and a coarse bracket does that. The thesis treats BLE
RSSI as a range BRACKET — enough to associate an advertisement with a zone —
never as a ranging signal.

fields.meaning: received power at distance d — what RSSI reports
power at a reference distance, measured once
path-loss exponent: 2 in free space, 3–5 indoors
random shadowing and multipath — tens of decibels indoors

figures.caption: The model and a plausible measurement of it. Scrubbing n shows how much of the curve is environment rather than physics — and the dashed line shows why inverting the model for a distance indoors is a bracket rather than a range: the fading term is worth several metres of apparent distance.
RSSI against CSI, as the sensing literature tabulates it. Every row is a reason CSI exists; the last row is the reason RSSI has not gone away.

cards.question:
RSSI — what is it, who computes it and when, and why is it both too coarse
and good enough?
cards.reading:
Received power falls with the logarithm of distance, at a rate set by the
environment, plus a random term that is the whole problem indoors.
cards.title: RSSI

cards.example:
What the primitive achieves, and why it is nevertheless the wrong tool here.

With the fine-timing-measurement protocol behind it, Wi-Fi Certified
Location claims **sub-metre** indoor accuracy on wide-bandwidth devices, and
ultra-wideband two-way ranging reaches **well under a metre** in high
multipath, because its short pulses resolve individual reflections.

There is even a counting result built on it: one paper collects RTT values to
every nearby access point and uses them as a FINGERPRINT for the number of
people in a room, rather than as ranges.

So the objection is not accuracy. It is that every one of those needs the
measured party's radio to answer an FTM request, and this thesis counts
people who carry nothing, install nothing and do nothing. A person who has
not opted in will never reply.
cards.explanation:
Round-Trip Time: send, wait for the reply, subtract the far end's turnaround,
halve, and multiply by the speed of light.

What it AVOIDS is the hard part of one-way timing: the two ends do not need
synchronised clocks, because t1 and t4 are measured by the same clock and
t2, t3 by the other. Only the DIFFERENCE at each end matters, so absolute
time never enters. That is why the 802.11 fine-timing-measurement protocol
is built this way, and why removing the responder's own processing delay
means transient queuing at the far side does not bias the distance.

The catch is scale, and it is the plot. Metre accuracy needs nanosecond
timing, and any processing delay at the far end must be known and subtracted
exactly. Wide bandwidth helps because it separates the direct path from its
echoes; narrow-band hardware cannot tell you whether the first arrival was
really the first.

It also needs a cooperating peer — the same dependency FTM has, and the same
reason we use neither. Surveyed as an alternative primitive, not implemented.

fields.meaning: departure and arrival, both measured by the SAME clock at the initiator
arrival and departure at the responder — its own turnaround
speed of light, about 0.3 metres per nanosecond
the one-way distance

figures.caption: The whole difficulty in one straight line. Light crosses 30 cm in a nanosecond, and the two-way halving makes that 15 cm of range error per nanosecond of timing error. Metre accuracy is a seven-nanosecond measurement.

markers.label: 1 m of error at about 6.7 ns

cards.question:
RTT — what is it, what does it avoid needing, and what is the catch
indoors?
cards.reading:
Take the total elapsed time at the initiator, subtract the far side's own
turnaround, halve it, and multiply by the speed of light.
cards.title: RTT

cards.back:
Receiver. In our deployment, nine of the ten nodes: monitor-mode listeners
extracting CSI from frames they were never meant to receive.

"Monitor mode" is the load-bearing detail. A station in normal mode discards
every frame not addressed to it, in hardware, before the host sees it. A
monitor interface keeps them all and prefixes each with a radiotap header,
which is what makes passive observation possible at all.
cards.example:
What a receiver's own kernel says about how much it is losing, read live off
node monad05. The monitor interface has taken in **203.4 million packets**
and DROPPED **34.1 million** of them — about **14%** — while its transmit
columns are all zero, because a listener never speaks.

Two things follow, and both are why RX count is a design decision rather
than a budget line.

Those drops are at the interface, before any of our code runs, so no
application-level delivery figure can see them. And a second node in the
same room on the same channel will not have the same number, because
dropping depends on that node's own load, its thermal state and its
scheduling. One monitor reports one number and cannot know it is one sample
of several.

figures.caption: Live from node monad05, 2026-08-26. `wlp1s0mon0` is the AX210 monitor interface: 203 million packets in, 34 million dropped, nothing transmitted. The base interface `wlp1s0` shows zeros because the capture runs on the monitor interface, not on it.

cards.front: RX — and why does it matter that we have nine of them rather than one?
cards.title: RX
cards.why:
The count is the contribution. A single monitor cannot see that two receivers
hearing the SAME transmitter on the SAME channel at the same moment disagree
— and ours disagree by around a dozen points of delivered fraction.

That spread is invisible to any single-monitor methodology, and no corpus
paper reports it because none operates an array that could. It matters
practically too: the remedy the literature prescribes for irregular sampling
was formed on single monitors at far lower rates, and whether it survives this
spread is an open question this instrument can actually answer.

cards.example:
Take a link with nothing moving and record four packets over a few seconds.
Overlay their phase curves and the plot above is what you get: four visibly
different lines, all with the same wiggle buried inside them.

Fit and subtract a straight line from each. The four collapse onto one
curve, and that curve is the channel. Nothing about the room changed between
the four packets — the difference between them was entirely instrument.

The alternative route to the same place, and the one our hardware makes
cheap: take the RATIO of two antennas on the same radio chain. Both antennas
share the oscillator and the converter, so both carry the same tilt, and
division cancels it exactly — no unwrapping, no fitting, no estimate. That is
why a 2 × 2 node gets usable phase and a single-antenna node does not.
cards.explanation:
Sampling Frequency Offset: the receiver's converter ticks at a slightly
different rate from the transmitter's, so samples are taken fractionally
early or late and the error compounds across the frame.

The useful fact is the SHAPE it produces: a phase error growing LINEARLY with
subcarrier index. That linearity is no coincidence — a time shift in one
domain is a phase ramp in the other, so a timing error can only ever appear
as a slope across frequency. Symbol timing offset produces the same slope for
the same reason, which is convenient: one fit removes both.

And it is what makes sanitisation tractable. Unwrap the phase across
subcarriers, fit a straight line, subtract it. You have removed the
instrument and kept the room, without ever knowing the offset itself.

What survives that fit is the non-linear part — the actual channel — and
what is lost is any absolute phase and any genuinely linear component of the
channel itself. That loss is accepted, because there is no way to tell a
linear channel term from a timing error with one packet.

fields.meaning: subcarrier index — the axis the error is linear in
sampling-time error, in samples; different on every packet
FFT size
a constant phase offset, absorbed by the same fit

figures.caption: Four packets, seconds apart, from the same unmoved link. The underlying shape never changes; the TILT changes on every packet. Scrub the frames and it is obvious why raw phase looks like noise and why a per-packet line fit recovers the room.

the straight line a fit removes

cards.question:
SFO — what is it, what shape does it leave in the data, and how do you get
rid of it?
cards.reading:
The measured phase is the true phase plus a term that grows in a straight
line with subcarrier index, plus a constant offset.
cards.title: SFO

cards.back:
System on Chip: processor cores, memory controller, graphics and peripheral
controllers on a single die, in one package. It is what a Raspberry Pi or a
phone is built around, as against a desktop where those parts are separate
chips on a board.

What is on ours and what is not is the load-bearing part. Our node is a
Raspberry Pi 5, whose SoC carries four Cortex-A76 cores at 2.4 GHz, the
memory controller and the peripheral interfaces. The **radio doing the
sensing is not on it**: the AX210 is a separate M.2 card reached over PCIe.
The Pi's own on-board WiFi chip is a different part again, and it cannot
produce CSI at all — which is exactly why the node needs the external card.

Three SoCs appear in this project and it is worth being able to tell them
apart: the Pi 5's, which HOSTS a CSI-capable radio; the ESP32-C5, whose SoC
contains its radio and exposes CSI through a documented API; and the
RTL8721DM, whose SoC contains a radio that computes channel information
internally and exposes none of it.
cards.example:
The two thermometers, and why confusing them would break the analysis.

Inside one experiment, the AX210's own front end sits at **61–64 °C** on
passively cooled nodes and **47 °C** on the fan-cooled ones — the fan removes
a roughly 16 °C offset from the radio. The SoC die is a different and hotter
story: two idle passively cooled nodes measured **70.5 °C** and **81.5 °C**,
and the second had already engaged its firmware soft limit with no headroom
left.

What the fan does NOT change is the daily swing: every node, cooled or not,
moves 7–10 °C on the NIC over 24 hours. So a thermal term in a drift model
has a DC part the fan removes and a diurnal part it does not, and only the
second is available as a within-session covariate.

Practical corollary: the fan splits the fleet into two thermal populations,
and a node can be silently throttled while every governor reading looks
healthy. Delivered record rate is not a witness — throttled and cooled nodes
returned the same rate on the same session, because the rate is
channel-limited rather than CPU-limited.

figures.caption: What is on the die and what is not. The sensing radio reaches the SoC over PCIe and has its own thermal environment, which is why "die temperature" and "radio temperature" are two different measurements.

nodes.label: AX210 — the sensing radio, NOT on the die

figures.caption: The three SoCs in this project, and what each does with the channel information its radio computes. The middle column is a hardware fact; the right-hand one is a firmware decision.
rows: **yes, and it is useless for CSI**
**only via the external AX210 and a patched driver**
yes — a documented vendor API, low resolution

cards.front:
SoC — what is it, what is on it and what is NOT, and why does a packaging
term appear in a measurement chapter?
cards.title: SoC
cards.why:
Because its TEMPERATURE turned out to be a covariate of the measurement, and
because the SoC's temperature is not the radio's.

Across a twelve-hour run the per-node phase-drift slope ordered perfectly
with mean die temperature on passively cooled nodes — a Spearman rank
correlation of −1.000 across five nodes, p = 0.0167, from the EXP-LIB-01
analysis. With five nodes that significance sits at the attainable floor and
the result turns on a fraction of a degree, so it is a strong monotone TREND
and a lead, not an established effect.

It is worth reporting because it suggests amplitude drift and phase drift
have different causes — one environmental, one thermal — which is a candidate
separation for the recalibration trigger. The fleet now holds a deliberate
20 °C contrast under a shared session to test it properly.

cards.example:
The method's home ground is brain–computer interfaces, and the parallel is
exact enough to be instructive. There, covariance matrices of EEG channels
from one subject in one session sit in a small region of the set; matrices
from a different subject or a different day sit somewhere else entirely, and
a classifier trained on the first fails on the second. Parallel transport
moves them into a common frame, and it works.

Substitute "environment" for "session" and that is our problem — which is
why it was a serious candidate rather than a straw man.

Why it nonetheless lost is worth stating plainly: transporting covariances
aligns SECOND-ORDER structure, and what our transfer gap mostly consists of
is a per-platform SCALE on the count mapping. Two labelled points fix a
scale directly. The elegant method was solving a harder problem than the one
we had.
cards.explanation:
Symmetric Positive Definite: the class covariance matrices belong to.
Symmetric because the covariance of a with b equals that of b with a, and
positive definite because no linear combination of the variables can have
negative variance — formally, xᵀPx > 0 for every non-zero x.

Those two conditions carve out a curved set, not a flat one. The consequence
is concrete: the entrywise average of two covariance matrices is generally
NOT the covariance a geometry-respecting average would give, and it can
distort determinants — the "swelling" effect. So a whole family of methods
exists to move covariance matrices between domains ALONG the set rather than
through the straight-line middle, with parallel transport as the standard
tool and an affine-invariant distance as the metric.

The invariance in the formula is what makes it attractive for transfer. The
distance is unchanged if BOTH matrices are transformed by the same invertible
map — a change of reference, a different sensor gain, a re-scaled recording.
Exactly the nuisance an encoding-level shift introduces.

We ran one, as one of four mathematically independent LABEL-FREE alternatives
tested under pre-registered kill lines. It recovered only a small share of
the cross-environment gap and lost to a plain scalar recalibration fitted on
two labelled anchors.

fields.meaning: two symmetric positive-definite matrices — here, two covariances
the whitening transform — "measured relative to P₁"
the matrix logarithm, which flattens the curved set locally
Frobenius norm — the root sum of squares of the entries

figures.caption: Why the straight line is wrong. The set of covariance matrices is a curved cone, so the entrywise average of two of them is a point the geometry does not put between them. The affine-invariant distance follows the geodesic instead.
The four label-free alternatives, run under pre-registered kill lines, against the two labelled anchors. Reported as run and lost — which is what a kill line is for.
rows: a small share of the gap
**worse than nothing — error more than doubled**

cards.question:
SPD — what is the class, why is averaging two of them entrywise wrong, and
where did it show up here?
cards.reading:
The distance between two covariance matrices is the size of the logarithm of
one whitened by the other — a distance along the curved set they live in,
not a straight line through the middle.
cards.title: SPD

cards.back:
Symbol Timing Offset: the receiver opens its FFT window slightly early or
late relative to the true symbol boundary. Because a time shift is a
frequency-domain phase ramp, the effect is again a slope across subcarriers.

Where it comes from: the receiver finds the symbol boundary by correlating
against the preamble, and that estimate is never exact. A guard interval
gives it slack — the window can be a little early without catching the
previous symbol's echoes — and being inside the slack is enough for
DECODING while still leaving a phase ramp that matters for SENSING.
cards.example:
The reason a decoder can be perfectly happy while a sensing pipeline is
ruined, in one comparison.

A decoder needs to tell one constellation point from another, so it tolerates
a phase error of a good fraction of the spacing between points. A sensing
pipeline is trying to detect a body that changes the channel phase by a few
tenths of a radian. A timing error well inside the decoder's tolerance is
several times the size of the effect being measured.

So the frame decodes, the link reports no errors, the driver logs nothing,
and the phase is unusable. Nothing is broken; the two applications simply
have tolerances two orders of magnitude apart. That is why phase sanitisation
is a step in every CSI pipeline and not a troubleshooting measure.

figures.caption: The four packet-varying contaminants, the shape each leaves, and the remedy. Two share a shape, which is why one line fit handles both — and the last one is removed by a ratio rather than by a fit.
rows: rotation growing with TIME within the frame
estimate and derotate, or antenna ratio
**linear ramp across SUBCARRIER — the same shape**
known per standard; or antenna ratio

cards.front: STO — what goes wrong, and what does it share with SFO?
cards.title: STO
cards.why:
It shares its SHAPE with sampling-frequency offset, which is convenient: one
line fit removes both. It is also why phase is treated as guilty until proven
innocent in CSI work while amplitude needs far less repair.

Together with carrier-frequency offset and cyclic-shift diversity these terms
vary packet to packet, so no fixed correction exists — sanitisation is an
estimation problem on every frame.

cards.example:
What a clock seam looks like in a result, which is the reason for the rule.

Suppose a session starts, and eleven minutes in the time daemon steps the
clock forward by two seconds. A reduction that assigns each record a
timestamp of "session start plus record index divided by rate" now places
every subsequent record two seconds early. Every derived quantity that
depends on time — Doppler, variance over a window, cross-node agreement —
sees an abrupt change at minute eleven, in every stream at once.

That looks exactly like something happening in the room. It is the clock.
Binning on each record's own timestamp makes the step visible as a two-second
gap, which is a gap you can drop, rather than as an event you might publish.
cards.explanation:
Time of Arrival: absolute travel time from transmitter to receiver. Unlike
round-trip timing it is one-way, so the subtraction crosses from one device's
clock to another's — and both must agree to within nanoseconds for the answer
to be a distance.

Our nodes cannot. They carry no real-time clock, so a node boots believing it
is some time in the past, and the time daemon may STEP the clock in the
middle of a session.

We discipline against one node of the fleet rather than a public source,
because the science needs relative coherence between observers more than
correct absolute time. That is a deliberate choice with a consequence every
reduction must respect: bin on each record's OWN timestamp, never on when the
session started, or a clock seam appears as a physical event.

fields.meaning: departure time, read from the TRANSMITTER's clock
arrival time, read from the RECEIVER's clock
speed of light — 0.3 metres per nanosecond
the one-way distance, if and only if the two clocks agree

figures.caption: One-way timing needs the two clocks to agree, because the subtraction crosses between them. Round-trip timing avoids this entirely by keeping each subtraction inside one clock — which is why it is the primitive the standard actually uses.

messages.label: stamps departure t₁ on ITS clock
frame in flight — about 3 ns per metre
stamps arrival t₂ on a DIFFERENT clock
d = (t₂ − t₁)c — valid only if the clocks agree

figures.caption: Our clock arrangement, and what each property costs. The last row is the rule every reduction must respect, and the reason is in the row above it.
rows: No real-time clock on the node
a node boots believing it is some time in the past
Time daemon may STEP the clock mid-session
**Disciplined against one fleet node, not a public source**
**relative coherence between observers is preserved; absolute time is not**

cards.question: ToA — state it, and say what it needs that we do not have.
cards.reading:
Distance is the arrival time minus the departure time, multiplied by the
speed of light — one way, one subtraction, two different clocks.
cards.title: ToA

cards.back:
Time of Flight: the propagation time itself. Time of Arrival is WHEN the
signal landed; time of flight is HOW LONG it took. In practice the terms are
used almost interchangeably, and both name the distance-from-delay primitive.

The family has four members and they differ in what they REQUIRE, not in the
physics. ToF/ToA needs two synchronised clocks. RTT needs one clock and a
cooperating peer. TDOA needs synchronised INFRASTRUCTURE and no clock at the
target. AoA needs a calibrated antenna array and no timing at all.
cards.example:
What goes wrong when the requirement is misread — three concrete failures,
each of which has an easily recognised symptom.

**Calling RTT "ToF" and dropping the turnaround term.** The far side's
processing delay stays in the number, so the distance reads long by however
busy that radio was. The symptom is a range that grows when the network gets
loaded, which looks like the target moving away.

**Using ToA with unsynchronised clocks.** The clock offset adds directly to
the delay, and light moves 0.3 m per nanosecond — a one-microsecond offset is
300 metres. The symptom is not a noisy distance; it is a confident, absurd
one.

**Using TDOA but synchronising the target instead of the anchors.** TDOA
works because the anchors share a clock and the target need not; get that
backwards and there is nothing left to difference.

Our own version of the same error class is smaller and real: binning records
on session-start time rather than on their own timestamps turns a clock step
into a physical-looking event.

figures.caption: Four ranging primitives, what each requires, and the symptom you get for confusing it with its neighbour. The right-hand column is what to recognise in somebody else's results.
rows: confident, absurd distances — 300 m per µs of offset
range grows with the far side's load
synchronised anchors; nothing at the target
nothing to difference; no fix at all
a bearing that points at the wall, not the source

cards.front:
ToF — same as ToA? And what actually goes wrong if you confuse the members
of this family?
cards.title: ToF
cards.why:
Worth knowing mainly so two words for one idea do not catch you out. Neither
is used here — we estimate how many, not where, and the fleet's clock
arrangement rules out one-way timing regardless.

cards.example:
Where it bites, and it bites us.

The drift-triggered recalibration rule was tested against a fixed schedule
for accuracy EQUIVALENCE, with the margin declared in advance. It **failed**.
So the thesis does not claim parity, and that is the whole point of having
run the test: a plain comparison would have found "no significant
difference" and the claim would have been parity.

What the thesis claims instead is what it can prove — the trigger spends
roughly half the calibration budget at a small accuracy cost. That is a cost
FRONTIER rather than a free lunch, and it is a more useful sentence to an
operator than a parity claim would have been: it tells them what they are
buying and what they are paying.
cards.explanation:
Two One-Sided Tests, the standard equivalence test. It asks "are these two
things close enough to be treated as the same?" by testing separately that
the difference is not meaningfully above, and not meaningfully below, a
margin declared in advance.

Why a plain test cannot ask it. An ordinary significance test can only FAIL
to find a difference, and failing to find one is not evidence there is none —
it might just mean too little data. Absence of evidence is not evidence of
absence, and with a small enough sample nothing is ever significant.
Equivalence testing inverts the burden of proof: it makes "the same" the
thing you have to demonstrate.

The practical form of that inversion is the picture. Instead of asking
whether the interval excludes zero, you ask whether the entire interval fits
inside ±Δ. More data narrows the interval, which HELPS an equivalence claim —
the opposite incentive to a significance test, and one worth having.

Declaring the margin BEFORE seeing the data is what makes the answer binding.
A margin chosen afterwards is a margin chosen to pass.

One honesty note: the vault's statistics corpus covers hypothesis testing,
intervals and two-sample tests, and holds no dedicated equivalence-testing
text. The formulation above is the standard one and is cited to nothing here
because there is nothing here to cite.

fields.meaning: the true difference between the two methods
the equivalence margin — declared BEFORE the data
the two one-sided nulls, each rejected at the chosen level
equivalence, which is a POSITIVE claim rather than a failure to find one

figures.caption: Equivalence has a picture, and it is not a p-value. The whole confidence interval must lie inside the declared margin. An interval straddling zero but reaching past Δ is exactly the case an ordinary test calls "no significant difference" and TOST calls undecided.

curves.label: upper end of the confidence interval
lower end of the confidence interval

markers.label: equivalent: the whole interval fits inside ±Δ

cards.question:
TOST — what question does it ask, why can a plain test not ask it, and what
happened when we ran one?
cards.reading:
Reject both one-sided nulls — that the difference is at least the margin, and
that it is at most minus the margin — and what remains is equivalence.
cards.title: TOST

cards.back:
Transmitter. One node of the ten, running as a paced illuminator: it emits
frames at a commanded rate that nobody associates to and nobody replies to.

"Commanded rate" is the phrase that matters. Because we choose how many
frames leave, we know the denominator of every delivery figure — and a
denominator nobody knows is the reason the field reports received counts
rather than delivered fractions.
cards.example:
The census the owned transmitter makes possible, on four nodes on
2026-08-23: **98.4% of commanded frames delivered**, and **15–16% of the
delivered records carrying an all-zero I/Q matrix** — a valid header, the
right payload length, a plausible RSSI, and no measurement inside. Useful
yield is therefore about **83%**.

Nothing in that sentence is available without owning the transmitter. A
passive study can count records; it cannot say what fraction of what was
sent they represent, so it cannot notice a fifteen-point gap between
"delivered" and "useful".

And the same ownership is what makes the paired-band contrast possible at
all. Because illumination is monitor-mode injection rather than an access
point, it works on BOTH bands — which is the experiment an AP-based
illuminator could not have produced on this hardware.

figures.caption: What owning the transmitter buys, measured. The first two rows are only knowable with a commanded denominator, and the gap between them is the number that matters.
rows: Records with an all-zero I/Q matrix
yes, but only as a share of what arrived
no — needs a common commanded stimulus

cards.front: TX — and what changes when you own it?
cards.title: TX
cards.why:
Owning the transmitter is what turns a deployment into an EXPERIMENT. It
fixes channel, band, modulation and rate, so the stimulus is a controlled
variable rather than whatever the building happened to send.

It also creates the reference that makes impairments measurable. Because we
know exactly how many frames were commanded, we can say what fraction
arrived — which is how delivery became a measurand rather than an assumption,
and how the rate ladder could show that delivery tracks competing channel
load rather than commanded rate.

cards.back:
The IEEE 802.11 family of wireless LAN standards. A certification brand
rather than a technology name, but universally used as one. It operates on
unlicensed spectrum around 2.4 GHz and between 5 and 5.8 GHz.
cards.example:
The trap, and the sentence that walks out of it.

A committee member says: "millimetre-wave radar would count this room
better." The wrong answer defends WiFi's accuracy. The right answer is one
sentence and a concession: "yes — and it costs a new device per room, an
installation, and a maintenance path. Our claim is that the channel estimate
is already being computed for communication in every room that has WiFi, so
the marginal cost of counting is near zero."

Then the honest limit, volunteered rather than extracted: the sensing
fidelity available from a communication waveform is bounded by design, and
integrated sensing theory says so formally. We are not claiming to beat a
radar. We are claiming a different point on a cost curve.

figures.caption: The comparison as the thesis actually makes it. Every column but the last favours a purpose-built sensor, which is why the argument is about the last column.

cards.front: WiFi — what is the deployment argument, stated without enthusiasm?
cards.title: WiFi
cards.why:
The argument for building on it is NOT that it senses well. Dedicated radar
senses better; cameras see more. The argument is twofold and narrow: it is
already in the building, and the channel estimate the sensing depends on is
already being computed for communication.

Marginal cost near zero, and no new device in anyone's room. That is the
whole deployment case, and overstating it is a defense trap — the honest
version concedes a purpose-built sensor would outperform this, and argues
cost and ubiquity instead.

cards.back:
Wireless Local Area Network: the scope 802.11 standardises. The 802.11bf
amendment adds a WLAN SENSING procedure so that a compliant device can be
ASKED for channel measurements alongside normal traffic.

The procedure names four ROLES, and they are the part worth learning, because
they do not have to be the same device. A **sensing initiator** starts the
measurement. A **sensing responder** takes part in it. A **sensing
transmitter** sends the sounding frame, and a **sensing receiver** measures
it. One device can hold several roles.

The exchange is then: negotiate a session, send a sounding announcement,
send the null-data sounding frame, and report the measurement back through a
defined interface. What the amendment standardises is not the physics — it is
the request, the schedule and the report format.
cards.example:
The same measurement, twice: how it is obtained today on our own node, and
how the amendment would obtain it.

Today it takes a purpose-built kernel driver, a monitor interface and a
capture service, and the resulting file's meaning is tied to that exact
chipset and driver version. Under 802.11bf the same measurement is a
REQUEST to a compliant device, with a defined report format — so a dataset
would carry its own interpretation, and a model trained on one vendor's
hardware would have a defined thing to expect from another's.

That is the difference between an exploit and an interface, and it is why the
thesis treats the amendment as the standardisation horizon rather than as a
feature.

figures.caption: The 802.11bf sensing procedure, in outline. The roles are separate from the devices: one station can be initiator and receiver at once, which is what lets a client rather than the access point drive a measurement.

messages.label: null data packet — the sounding frame
reports the measurement in a defined format

figures.caption: Today's route, as commands. No output is shown because it is driver-specific by construction — which is the point being made: every step here is a local arrangement, and the amendment's purpose is to replace the whole column with one request.

steps.note: What this chipset admits to supporting. Nothing here mentions sensing — CSI is not a standardised capability yet.
A monitor interface, because a station discards frames not addressed to it before the host sees them.
steps.run: iw dev wlp1s0 interface add wlp1s0mon0 type monitor

steps.note: The patched driver is what exposes the channel estimate. Unpatched, the number is computed and thrown away.
Our own capture service. Under 802.11bf this whole sequence collapses into a negotiated measurement request.

figures.caption: Where the two routes differ. Only the last row is a research problem — the rest is plumbing that a standard would remove.

cards.front:
WLAN — what does 802.11bf add to it, how does the procedure work, and what
is its status?
cards.title: WLAN
cards.why:
It matters because it would make sensing hardware-agnostic. Today CSI access
depends on patched firmware and reverse-engineered drivers, and every dataset
is bound to the chipset that produced it — which is the root of the field's
reproducibility problem.

Status has to be stated honestly: the amendment is in final ratification and
early commercialisation, so interoperable CSI sensing is a PROSPECTIVE
capability. Our experimental work runs on pre-standard commodity hardware and
the thesis says so.

choices: Access Point — yes, the fleet runs dual-band APs on 2.4 and 5 GHz.
Access Point — but the fleet has none. Intel firmware blocks 5 GHz transmit-master, so illumination is monitor-mode injection on both bands.
Access Point — the fleet runs 5 GHz APs only, since 2.4 GHz is too congested.
Access Point — the phones act as the APs during a session.
cards.example:
The shape of this question recurs, so learn the shape rather than the answer:
**a term is asked, and the interesting part is that our deployment does not
contain the thing.**

Three more in the same family. "Which band do your APs beacon on?" — none;
there is no beacon. "How do phones associate?" — they do not; there is
nothing to associate to, and a quest step that asked them to would block on
an association that cannot happen. "What is your AP's transmit power?" —
the illuminator's, and it is an injector rather than an AP.

Each time, the honest answer names the constraint (Intel's regulatory
mechanism blocks 5 GHz transmit-master on this card family), then names what
was gained (injection works on both bands, so the paired-band contrast
survived). A constraint plus a consequence is a design decision. A
constraint alone sounds like an accident.
cards.explanation:
There is no access point in this deployment, and the reason is a vendor
constraint rather than a preference: Intel's regulatory mechanism blocks
transmit-master on 5 GHz for every client card of this family, and forcing it
past the kernel crashes the CSI backport. Monitor-mode injection works on
BOTH bands, which restores the paired-band contrast an access-point
illuminator would have foreclosed. The first option is the answer a reader of
