by the mean is what the derivation prescribes. There is a second, blunter
reason: |H| is AGC-relative, so an absolute variance is not comparable
across captures or across receivers, and a mean-scaled one is much closer
to being so. This feature is the workhorse of the whole thesis — it is the
quantity in the partial-pooling calibration model, and it is the one whose
count relation is sign-stable across all seven environments while its
scale is platform-stratified.

fields.meaning: standard deviation of amplitude over the window
mean amplitude over the same window

figures.caption: Two sweeps in one picture. Along the axis the receiver's gain changes and the raw spread follows while CV does not. Across the frames the ROOM changes — and CV moves only then. That is what "comparable between receivers" means.

curves.label: raw standard deviation — moves with gain
raw standard deviation — moves with gain
raw standard deviation — moves with gain
raw standard deviation — moves with gain

cards.question:
Write the workhorse counting feature and justify its normaliser from the
model rather than from convenience.
cards.reading:
The coefficient of variation of CSI amplitude: its standard deviation
divided by its mean, over a window.
cards.title: The counting feature

cards.example:
Balance a real room's doorway and watch the equation do arithmetic.

Our measurement space is about **48 m²**. Suppose people enter at 2.0 per
second and leave at 1.5, so the net inflow is 0.5 per second. Spread over the
floor, the density rises at 0.5 / 48 ≈ **0.0104 ped/m² per second** — so it
takes about **96 seconds** to add one person per square metre, and about
**170 seconds** to go from empty to Weidmann's capacity density.

That is the conservation law being useful: it converts door counts into a
density field, with no model of how anyone walks.

And the limit that retired it as a PRIOR: the equation constrains ρ through
the divergence of ρv, and indoors the mean velocity field is close to zero
with a noisy divergence. Matched, constant and ANTI-PHYSICAL closures gave
identical error, while plain smoothing beat all three. What survives is the
density field as the estimation TARGET.
cards.explanation:
It follows from mass conservation under the HOMOGENEOUS-VELOCITY
assumption — everyone in an infinitesimal volume shares one mean velocity
— and it is the first-order LWR scalar conservation law. As a kinematic
identity it is exact. The thesis's contribution here is a documented
negative: imposed as a training-time regulariser it does NOT beat generic
smoothing on indoor geometry. A mismatched-closure ablation is what
settled it — a physically correct closure, a constant closure and an
ANTI-PHYSICAL closure gave identical high-density error, while plain
smoothing beat all three. A conservation term whose benefit survives
replacing the conservation law with its opposite is not acting as physics.
What survives is the density field as the estimation TARGET.

fields.meaning: crowd density field, people per square metre
bulk velocity field
pedestrian flux
local rate of density change

figures.caption: The whole content of the conservation law in one picture: no sources, no sinks. It is exact as a bookkeeping identity — which is precisely why it turned out to add nothing when used as a training penalty.

nodes.label:
a patch of floor
density ρ
ρ rises only if more comes in than goes out — nobody appears from nowhere

cards.question:
Write the continuity equation for a pedestrian continuum, name the
assumption that closes it, and state what this thesis did with it.
cards.reading:
Density at a point changes only through net flux divergence — no sources,
no sinks.
cards.title: The conservation law

cards.example:
Evaluate the closure at three densities and the fundamental diagram stops
being abstract.

At **0.5 ped/m²**: u = 1.30 m/s, so flow is 0.65 per metre per second — a
2 m doorway passes about 2.6 people a second. At **1.75**, the fit's
capacity: u = 0.70, flow **1.23**, about 2.5 a second. At **4.0**: u = 0.16,
flow 0.63, about 1.3 a second.

Three times the density for no extra throughput, then eight times the density
for half of it. The door cannot tell those rooms apart; the density can.

Two honesty notes travel with the numbers. The 1.34 m/s free speed is a
metastudy fit, and measured free speeds spread from about 1.10 m/s for groups
of six to 1.64 m/s at a bottleneck. And the empirical capacity density across
independent studies is a RANGE, roughly 1.3 to 2.3, not the single value the
fitted curve happens to peak at.
cards.explanation:
Without a closure the continuity equation holds two unknown fields, ρ and
v, and cannot be integrated forward. The fundamental diagram resolves the
underdetermination by making speed a single-valued function of density.
Two things to be exact about. First, the free-flow value is 1.34 m/s — the
1.5 to 1.6 m/s figures in speed-prediction papers are congested-diagram
asymptotes, and quoting one as v₀ mixes two quantities. Second, the closure
is the only component the thesis treats as portable-and-refittable; the
eikonal direction field, obstacle geometry, corridor widths and exit
boundary conditions also change between venues and must be re-specified
separately.

fields.meaning: mean walking speed at density ρ (m/s)
free-flow desired speed (m/s)
jam density (ped/m²), where speed reaches zero
shape parameter of the Weidmann closure

figures.caption: Speed falls monotonically; flux is concave and peaks near 2 ped/m². Past capacity, more density means LESS throughput.

cards.question:
Write the Weidmann closure, and say why the continuum model cannot be
integrated without something of this shape.
cards.reading:
Walking speed falls from the free-flow value towards standstill as density
rises to the jam density.
cards.title: The fundamental diagram

cards.example:
Invert it once and the bracket becomes obvious. Reference −40 dBm at one
metre, exponent n = 3.5, measurement **−70 dBm** → about **7.2 m**.

Now admit the shadowing term. Indoor multipath and body absorption routinely
move RSSI by more than **10 dB** over a small displacement, and at n = 3.5
ten decibels is a factor of **1.9 in distance**. The same measurement is
consistent with anywhere from roughly 4 m to 14 m.

So we ask it a question it can answer. "Is this advertiser in the north
reading room or the south one?" — two zones 15 m apart, and a 10 dB
uncertainty rarely swaps them. "How far away is it?" — unanswerable, and any
system claiming otherwise indoors is reporting its model rather than its
measurement.
cards.explanation:
The whole point is what this DOES NOT support. The exponent varies with
building materials, furniture and obstruction; multipath swings RSSI by
tens of decibels over small displacements; and bodies at 2.4 GHz absorb
and reflect in ways that depend on posture and orientation. A single
instantaneous reading is therefore a poor proxy for distance. The thesis
treats BLE RSSI as a COARSE RANGE BRACKET — enough to associate an
advertisement with a spatial zone and anchor a count — and never as a
ranging signal. Its own Fresnel-geometry analysis bounds this further: a
metre-grade BLE position may gate which link's sensitive region a body
occupies, and can never predict per-zone phase.

fields.meaning: transmitter–receiver distance
reference distance (commonly 1 m)
path-loss exponent — 2 in free space, above 4 when cluttered
zero-mean Gaussian shadowing term

figures.caption: The exponent is not a universal constant — it doubles between free space and a cluttered room, so it needs per-environment calibration.

cards.question:
Write the log-distance path-loss model and say what it is good for in this
architecture — and what it is not.
cards.reading:
Received level falls logarithmically with distance, at a rate set by the
path-loss exponent, plus a random shadowing term.
cards.title: The BLE range primitive

cards.example:
Take τ = 6 hours and read the weight as an operator would.

One hour after an anchoring, w = e^(−1/6) = **0.85**: the estimate is still
mostly anchored. At six hours w = **0.37**. At twelve hours w = **0.14**. At
a full day w = **0.018** — the anchor is contributing essentially nothing and
the system is running on the CSI model alone.

That curve is what "staleness" means quantitatively, and it is why (T*, ε)
is a PAIR: the interval you can tolerate depends entirely on how much error
you accept once the weight has decayed.

The correct reading of the formula matters as much as the number. Written as
an exponential decay it looks like a heuristic knob. It is the Kalman gain
trajectory of a recursive filter over a slowly drifting state — so τ is a
statement about the drift process, not a tuning preference.
cards.explanation:
Read naively this is a heuristic. Read correctly it is the KALMAN GAIN
TRAJECTORY of a recursive Bayesian filter over a slowly-drifting
calibration state: BLE supplies a rare low-variance measurement of the
count, CSI a frequent higher-variance one whose calibration drifts, and
the optimal estimator's gain does exactly this. That reading is Pillar 3,
and it unifies two mechanisms the thesis first developed separately —
fusion is the filter's gain, and the recalibration trigger is a sequential
change-point rule on the filter's innovation. Note what the simulation
actually showed: a naive CONSTANT blend is dominated. The complementarity
is in TIME, not in density — an earlier density-axis formulation of this
claim was retired.

fields.meaning: elapsed time since the last calibration anchor
staleness time constant of the deployment
confidence weight on the anchor versus the CSI estimate

figures.caption: Fresh anchor: the absolute reference dominates. Stale anchor: the continuous relative sensor does. The switch tracks the lower envelope of the two error curves.
figures.x_label: Δt — time since the last anchor (units of τ)

cards.question:
Write the fusion weight, and say what it really is in the state-space
reading.
cards.reading:
The weight given to the device-count anchor decays exponentially with the
time since that anchor was taken.
cards.title: Pillar 3 — the staleness switch

cards.example:
Pin the formula on our own measured point and it starts predicting.

The headline result is that **two anchors recover about 42%** of the transfer
gap. Set w = k/(k + κ) with k = 2 and w = 0.42, and κ ≈ **2.8**. That single
fitted number now says what more anchors would buy: **four** anchors give
w ≈ 0.59, **eight** give w ≈ 0.74, and **twenty** give 0.88.

Two things follow, and this is exactly what a pillar is for. The measurement
is no longer an isolated 42% — it is one point on a curve with a mechanism
behind it. And the curve says the first two anchors are the bargain: going
from two to four buys 17 points, while going from eight to twenty buys 14
points for twelve times the labelling effort.

If a future site measured 42% at two anchors and only 45% at eight, the
mechanism would be wrong — which is the useful kind of wrong.
cards.explanation:
This is the formal spine of the flagship result. Cross-environment
counting is ONE partial-pooling model: a shared crowd-to-signal link with
per-environment parameters nested under a hardware group. The curve's
concavity is the prediction — recovery versus anchor count rises steeply
then flattens — and the measured leave-one-environment-out result matches
it. Four mathematically independent LABEL-FREE alternatives were run under
pre-registered kill lines and all lost to two anchors, for a reason
domain-adaptation theory names in advance: the dominant error is a
session-structural offset that is not identifiable from the unlabelled
target marginal. No label-free objective can remove it. A local labelled
reference can.

fields.meaning: number of labelled anchors in the new environment
prior strength — how many anchors the population is worth
estimate from the local anchors alone
population-level estimate pooled across environments

figures.caption: Steep at the start, flat later. The first two anchors buy most of what any number of anchors can buy — which is the closed-form reason the two-anchor result is not luck.
figures.x_label: k — labelled anchors in the new environment

cards.question:
Write the empirical-Bayes shrinkage estimator for a new environment, and
say what its shape predicts about anchor count.
cards.reading:
A new environment's parameter is a weighted blend of its own few labels
and the population prior, with the weight rising as anchors accumulate.
cards.title: Pillar 1 — shrinkage

cards.example:
One room, two hours apart, same sensor, and the conversion moves in both
directions.

**During the lecture**: 30 people, most with a phone awake and a laptop on
the desk. Say the device channel observes D = 31 while r·p ≈ 1.15; the
correct estimate is 31 / 1.15 ≈ **27**. Assume r·p = 1 instead and you report
**31** — an overcount of four on a room of twenty-seven.

**During the exam**: 30 people, phones in bags with radios asleep. Now
D might be 14 with r·p ≈ 0.5, so the correct estimate is **28** and the
naive one is **14** — half the room.

Nothing about the room, the sensor or the people changed. A behaviour changed,
and it moved the conversion factor by more than a factor of two within two
hours. That is why r·p is identified jointly rather than imported from a
citation, and why the participant protocol sets penetration to one in Phase I
so that the product is measurable at all.
cards.explanation:
Only the PRODUCT is identified, which is why it is reported as one scalar
rather than two: in the swept grid r·p explains most of the variance in
recalibrated count error, with a helpful band around unity. An anchor that
miscounts devices is worse than no anchor at all — the plot's left-hand
blow-up is that statement. The conventional remedy is to import a
published conversion factor and hope it holds; the thesis rejects that
twice over, because the factor is non-stationary across crowd TYPES, and
because a point correction converts an unknown bias into a confident
number. Instead the ratio is a jointly identified latent, and its residual
uncertainty is PROPAGATED — it widens the predictive distribution rather
than shifting a point estimate.

fields.meaning: estimated number of people
observed device or identifier count
detection rate — the fraction of present devices actually seen
penetration — the fraction of people carrying a detectable device

figures.caption: The error blows up as r·p falls below one and flattens above it. The helpful band sits around unity — which is what the participant protocol is designed to occupy.

cards.question:
Write the conversion from a device count to a headcount, and say why the
thesis calls the denominator a sufficient statistic.
cards.reading:
The headcount estimate is the observed device count divided by the product
of detection rate and device-carriage penetration.
cards.title: The device-to-person conversion

cards.example:
What the guarantee is worth in practice, and what it does not settle.

Place ten receivers greedily on a floor — each time, add the one that covers
most of what is still uncovered. The theorem says the result covers at least
**63%** of what the best possible ten would have covered. Nobody computes the
best possible ten: for a hundred candidate positions there are more than
seventeen trillion sets of ten.

So the bound converts an intractable search into a loop, with a number you
can quote to a facilities manager.

What it does not settle is which objective to greedily optimise. Covering the
paths people TAKE and concentrating sensing on the busy HUB are different
submodular functions, so coverage-optimal and counting-optimal layouts differ
and neither dominates. And our own negative sits here: room-adjacency
structure looked like it should predict recoverability and did not — what did
was receiver density and placement, which is what this objective is about.
cards.explanation:
The two properties are MONOTONICITY — adding a sensor never reduces
coverage — and SUBMODULARITY — the marginal gain of adding one shrinks as
the set grows. Both were measured on this problem rather than assumed:
the placement objective came out exactly monotone submodular with zero
violations across the tested pairs. The result that earns the pillar is
not the bound itself but what the framing exposes: covering the paths
people take and concentrating sensing on the busy hub are DIFFERENT
submodular objectives, so coverage-optimal and counting-optimal placements
are provably distinct and neither dominates. That turns a descriptive
blind-spot figure into a placement objective with a proof.

fields.meaning: coverage objective over a set of placed sensors
the set greedy placement produces
the optimal set of the same size
the Nemhauser–Wolsey–Fisher bound

figures.caption: The bound tightens to 1 - 1/e from above as the budget grows. For a small sensor budget the guarantee is better than the famous number.

cards.question:
State the approximation guarantee greedy sensor placement carries, and the
two properties it needs.
cards.reading:
Greedily adding the sensor with the largest marginal coverage gets you at
least about 63 per cent of the best possible set.
cards.title: Pillar 4 — the greedy guarantee

cards.example:
Why the thesis reports this metric AND refuses to report only it, on five
windows.

Model A misses by 2, 2, 2, 2, 2 — MAE **2.0**. Model B misses by
0, 0, 0, 0, 10 — MAE **2.0**. Identical here, and completely different to an
operator: A is a steady bias you can correct, B is four right answers and one
evacuation-scale error.

The squared metric separates them (RMSE 2.0 against 4.5), which is the
argument FOR reporting a second metric — and the argument for absolute error
as the primary one is the reverse case: a single bad window caused by a gain
step or a clock seam should not dominate a whole evaluation.

And the measured reason one metric is not enough: under environment shift the
point and distributional contracts score nearly the same MAE, and separate
sharply on band-level scoring and calibration. A results table with one
column would have concluded that the output contract does not matter.
cards.explanation:
MAE stays for two reasons: comparability with a literature that reports
it, and because a distribution's mean must not be allowed to drift
unnoticed. But it is NOT sufficient, and the thesis proves that
empirically rather than stylistically. Scored on MAE alone the point and
distributional output contracts are nearly indistinguishable under
environment shift; scored on band ranked-probability score and calibration
error they are not remotely so, and it is the latter pair that tracks
whether a deployment moved to a new room can be trusted. A metric set
reporting only MAE would have CONCEALED the single clearest
cross-environment result the thesis holds.

fields.meaning: estimated count for window i
true count for window i
number of scored windows

figures.caption: Absolute error charges a mistake in proportion to its size; squared error charges a big mistake far more. On a 0–10 count range that difference decides which estimator wins.

cards.question:
Write mean absolute error, and say why the thesis keeps it while insisting
it is not sufficient.
cards.reading: The mean of the unsigned differences between estimated and true counts.
cards.title: Why the metric is absolute, not squared

cards.back:
Three first-class axes in frontmatter: confidence (0–100), novelty
(0–100 vs a NAMED prior-art anchor), and a one-line promotion gate.
Standing rule: priority = confidence × novelty; high-confidence but
low-novelty hypotheses are PREMISES to cite, not claims to defend.
cards.front: How is every thesis hypothesis evaluated and prioritised?
cards.title: The evaluation axes

cards.back:
Chosen, strength STRONG (confidence 90, novelty 25) — the only "strong"
in the portfolio: CSI temporal amplitude variance rises with occupancy,
confirmed on two independent real datasets + sim. Low novelty = it is
the field's premise; its job is to carry the calibration architecture
built on top. Gate: first-party replication + drift guard.
cards.front: occupancy-csi-variance — state, strength, and why it anchors everything.
cards.title: The anchor result

cards.back:
Chosen, plausible (confidence 72, novelty 85) — the highest-novelty core
bet: periodic BLE campaigns keep a drifting CSI count model honest. Real
motivation exists (42% cross-env recovery) but no public dataset has
synchronized BLE + CSI + counts. Gate: the IP-106 multi-week ≥2-site
periodic-vs-one-shot with live BLE anchors.

cards.back:

sufficient ground truth for calibrating CSI counting (count-without-
identify). Gate: IP-106 paired BLE-vs-headcount across crowd types —
R² ≥ 0.7 with a stable penetration ratio.

cards.back:
Chosen, supported (confidence 82, novelty 45): count information lives
in temporal/Doppler-shaped features, not static fingerprints. Fed by the

(only Doppler spectral SHAPE was above chance). Gate: first-party

cards.back:
Chosen, supported (confidence 78, novelty 60): robustness follows the
FEATURE TYPE (fingerprint vs kinematic), not the modality — fingerprints
break under layout change while kinematic features transfer. SCOPE
LIMIT: same-geometry only. The cross-geometry extension was REFUTED —

cards.back:

(platform-stratified CV bands in the 7-env pool). Gate: paired same-room

cards.back:
The pilot's ρ = 0.93 [0.72, 1.0] did not replicate at power: the powered
run gave ρ = 0.68 and FAILED TOST vs the oracle — so "≈ oracle" was

candidate → chosen → (deferred | superseded | refuted); strength runs
speculative → plausible → supported → strong. Promotion to chosen
requires the hypothesis's proving evidence to land in an argument-chain
claim (chain proves: list); transitions go through hypothesis_transition
so the ledger stays consistent.
cards.front: Name the hypothesis lifecycle states and the promotion mechanism.

Lifecycle state records the decision history — candidate, chosen,
deferred, refuted, superseded. Evidence strength records what the claim
has earned — speculative, plausible, supported, strong.

cards.title: Portfolio shape
cards.why:
They are deliberately orthogonal. A claim can be firmly chosen and only
plausible, and a claim central to an early draft can be honestly retired
once its refutation condition fires. Collapsing the two axes into one
number is how a portfolio starts lying about itself.

cards.back:
BLE occupies 40 × 2 MHz channels in 2.4 GHz; three of them (37, 38, 39)
are dedicated advertising channels spread across the band to dodge Wi-Fi.
Advertisers broadcast short packets on all three per event; scanners hop
between them. Localization typically consumes the RSSI of these
advertisements.
cards.front: How does BLE advertising work at the radio level?
cards.title: BLE advertising

cards.back:
Invert the log-distance model: d = d0·10^((PL0 − RSSI)/(10n)). Limits:
fading makes instantaneous RSSI ±5–10 dB noisy, n is environment-
dependent, bodies/orientation shadow the signal, and TX-power/antenna
variation across devices shifts the intercept. Meter-level indoors only
with aggregation.
cards.front: How does RSSI-based ranging work and what limits it?
cards.title: RSSI ranging

cards.back:
Geometric methods invert a propagation model per anchor (no survey, but
model-error-limited indoors). Fingerprinting matches a live vector against
a surveyed radio map (captures multipath structure, so more accurate —
but the map goes stale when the environment changes: the drift problem).
cards.front: Fingerprinting vs geometric (trilateration) localization — the trade?
cards.title: Fingerprinting vs geometry

cards.back:
(1) Ground truth: BLE devices provide an automated coarse count
(count-without-identify) that labels CSI data without cameras or manual
counting. (2) Calibration reference: periodic BLE campaigns re-anchor the
drifting CSI→count mapping. Cheap continuous BLE monitoring triggers
expensive recalibration.
cards.front: What TWO roles does BLE play in the thesis architecture?
cards.title: BLE roles in the thesis

choices: Privacy (count-without-identify), existing infrastructure/devices, and no line-of-sight or lighting requirements
BLE counts are more accurate than camera counts in all conditions
Cameras cannot operate at 2.4 GHz
BLE localizes every person to centimetre accuracy
cards.explanation:
BLE gives a privacy-preserving automated count from infrastructure that
is already there; it is NOT more accurate than cameras — its sufficiency
as ground truth is itself a hypothesis (ble-ground-truth-sufficiency,
gate: paired BLE-vs-headcount, R² ≥ 0.7).
cards.question: Why BLE instead of cameras for CSI ground truth?
cards.title: Why BLE for ground truth

cards.back:
The co-registered anchor resolves PRESENCE robustly (empty vs occupied,
effect size d = 2.3–3.7, noise-robust) but SATURATES — no graded
headcount. Presence ≠ count. Anchor placement, not anchor existence, is
the lever.
cards.front:
What did the co-registration campaign show about a BLE anchor's counting
ability in a multiroom layout?
cards.title: Anchor saturation

cards.back:
Partially. Concentrating anchors on the corridor hub (highest-betweenness
cell) + large rooms flipped the trend from +0.08 to −0.48 dB/person, made
all seeds' ρ negative, and resolved coarse steps (ΔN ≥ 4) — but fine
ΔN = 2 stayed unresolved. Design input for the hardware protocol:
concentrate anchors on hubs, not periphery.
cards.front:
Did topology-informed anchor placement recover the graded count that
dispersed placement lost?
cards.title: Placement recovery

cards.back:
BLE. In the topology campaign its location fingerprints were roughly two
and a half times more separable than CSI's per-link fingerprints.
cards.front:
For LOCATION fingerprinting, which wins — narrowband BLE RSSI at many
anchors, or wideband CSI at few links?
cards.title: BLE vs CSI fingerprints
cards.why:
Anchor count beats bandwidth for this task, which is exactly why BLE
earns its place as the calibration side-channel rather than as a rival
counting modality.

choices: When the model is geometry-mismatched — few-anchor affine re-anchoring overfits (K=3 gave 2.39×, worse than 1.48× zero-shot) and cannot fix a wrong model shape
It never fails; any anchor count helps
Only when BLE and CSI share the same band
When more than 10 anchors are used
cards.explanation:
Cross-geometry in-silico: K=3 → 2.39×, K=5 → 1.80× (both WORSE than
zero-shot 1.48×); only K=10 → 1.40× helped, and the one floor with a real
gap stayed broken. Affine re-anchoring is the wrong tool for geometry
mismatch — converges with the "switch, not fixed-gain blend" finding.
cards.question: When does affine BLE recalibration of a CSI count model FAIL?
cards.title: Affine recalibration limits

cards.back:
One Kalman filter over [count, calibration_bias]: CSI observes count+bias
every step, BLE observes count at campaigns. The fusion weight IS the
Kalman gain; the trigger IS sequential change-point detection (CUSUM) on
the cross-modal disagreement; recalibrate-now is optimal stopping.
cards.front:
In the state-space view, what do "fusion weight" and "recalibration
trigger" become?
cards.title: Kalman-style fusion

cards.back:
The cross-modal DISAGREEMENT between independently calibrated CSI→count
and BLE→count estimates tracks true error (pilot Spearman 0.93; powered
replication 0.68). CSI-only distribution monitoring (KS on features)
false-fires on 17% of error-irrelevant shifts — feature shift ≠ model
degradation.
cards.front:
Which statistic detects CSI model drift, and which plausible alternative
false-alarms?
cards.title: Drift detection statistic

choices: Parity on error at roughly one quarter of the calibration spend — condition-based maintenance, not error reduction
It beats fixed cadence on error at matched budget
It eliminates the need for calibration entirely
It halves the error at double the spend
cards.explanation:
At matched budget even a perfect-knowledge trigger did NOT beat evenly
spaced recalibration on error (0.421 vs 0.399) — scheduled recal also
fixes below-threshold drift. The payoff is parity at ~¼ the spend (2.0 vs
8.0 recals across a 4-zone estate). Never claim "event-driven beats
fixed."
cards.question:
What is the honest payoff of the drift-triggered recalibration policy vs
a fixed calendar cadence?
cards.title: Trigger economics

cards.back:
Disagreement is symmetric — it cannot tell stale-anchor from wrong-CSI. A
fresh BLE anchor can be wrongly diluted by CSI noise in a purely
condition-modulated fusion. Deployable answer: hybrid clock-GATED
freshness + condition-MODULATED staleness; log both the disagreement and
the anchor age.
cards.front:
Why can't the cross-modal disagreement statistic alone decide WHICH
modality is wrong?
cards.title: Symmetry limitation

cards.back:
CSI-based crowd counting has a mechanism that travels but a scale that
does not: a formal four-pillar theory (hierarchical calibration,
scattering saturation, state-space fusion, spectral+coverage) explains
why, predicts the empirical results already in hand, and prescribes the
BLE-calibrated architecture that keeps deployed models honest.
cards.front: State the thesis in one sentence, theory-first.
cards.title: The reframe

cards.back:
"Mechanism travels, scale doesn't" = a partial-pooling random-effects
model: a shared count→variance link with per-environment (and nested
per-platform) scale parameters. Recalibration = empirical-Bayes
shrinkage of a new environment's parameters toward the population prior;
anchor placement = Bayesian-optimal design.
cards.front: Pillar 1 (hierarchical calibration): claim and formal object?
cards.title: Pillar 1 — statement

cards.back:
(1) Slope sign-stable in 100% of environments but scale platform-
stratified: dispersion 0.96 flat → 0.28 within-platform. (2) EB shrinkage
with k = 2 anchors gives MAE 1.23 ≈ the independently measured 2-anchor
recalibration 1.32 — "42% with 2 anchors" reproduced as shrinkage, not
luck. (3) Nested prior tightens every endpoint: zero-shot 1.97 → 1.49
(beating the log-affine LOEO 1.75), k=2 → 1.13, oracle → 0.88.
cards.front: The three real-data confirmations of Pillar 1 (n = 939, 7 environments)?
cards.title: Pillar 1 — evidence

cards.back:
Model CSI as a sum of independent random phasors, one per mover; CLT
gives amplitude-variance growth that saturates: Var ≈ σ²(1 − e^(−K/K0)).
Predicts presence-easy/counting-hard AND the 5 GHz > 2.4 GHz band
ordering as wavelength effects — the empirical facts become theorems.
cards.front: Pillar 2 (scattering saturation): derivation and law?
cards.title: Pillar 2 — statement

cards.back:
(1) Concave-saturating beats linear by AIC in 5/7 counting-band
environments — WiMANS 5 GHz rooms unanimous (ΔAIC 45–95) with saturation
genuinely in-range (K0/Kmax 0.26–0.52); the 2 linear holdouts reported
honestly. (2) Band ordering 5 > 2.4 GHz by Cohen's d in 3/3 rooms (216
extra 2.4 GHz WiMANS files pulled to close the leg). One leg from
"strong": low-density Var ∝ K on first-party hardware.
cards.front: Pillar 2's two real-data confirmations?
cards.title: Pillar 2 — evidence

cards.back:
A Kalman filter over state [count, calibration_bias]: CSI measures
count + bias continuously, BLE measures count at campaigns. Fusion weight
= the Kalman gain; drift trigger = CUSUM change-point detection on
cross-modal disagreement; when-to-recalibrate = optimal stopping with a
cost knob.
cards.front:
Pillar 3 (state-space fusion): what single object unifies fusion,
trigger, and recalibration?
cards.title: Pillar 3 — statement

cards.back:
In-silico: filter MAE 0.53 vs best constant blend 0.84 vs CSI-only 1.53;
CUSUM reaches calendar parity at budget ratio 0.38 (≈¼, matching the
campaign); innovation-tracks-error ρ = 0.97 (campaign pilot 0.93).
Caveat: all synthetic-drift corpus — it stays candidate until the real
drift leg lands. Modelling lesson: trigger on raw cross-modal
disagreement with CURRENT BLE, not the whitened KF innovation.
cards.front: Pillar 3's supporting numbers, and why does it honestly stay a candidate?
cards.title: Pillar 3 — evidence and caveat

cards.back:
(4a) A STILL crowd's count is a spectral moment: amplitude variance
starves (breathing power buried under noise) but off-DC Doppler
line-counting recovers it. (4b) Sensor placement is monotone submodular
coverage maximisation — greedy achieves ≥ 1 − 1/e; counting-optimal and
coverage-optimal placements genuinely differ (Pareto front).
cards.front: Pillar 4 (spectral + coverage): the two linked claims?
cards.title: Pillar 4 — statement

cards.back:
In the STILL regime the off-DC Doppler peak-count feature clearly beats
amplitude variance, because variance starves when nobody moves. In the
MOVING regime variance already explains almost everything and the
spectral feature adds nothing. The two pillars partition by regime rather
than compete.
cards.front:
Pillar 4: how do the spectral feature and the variance feature partition
by regime, and what feature-design detail decided it?
cards.title: Pillar 4a — numbers
cards.why:
The design detail mattered: band-power SUMS drown in broadband noise.
COUNT the spectral lines instead.

choices: Parity-at-¼-budget → Pillar 2 (scattering saturation)
42% recovery with 2 anchors → Pillar 1 (EB shrinkage)
Presence easy, counting hard → Pillar 2 (concave variance law)
5 GHz > 2.4 GHz → Pillar 2 (wavelength prediction)
cards.explanation:
Parity-at-¼-budget belongs to Pillar 3 (optimal stopping / CUSUM
economics), not Pillar 2. The other three pairings are correct — knowing
which result is evidence for which pillar is exactly what a committee
probes.
cards.question:
Which empirical finding is EXPLAINED BY which pillar? Match the odd one
out.
cards.title: Cross-pillar unification

cards.back:
P1 hierarchical-calibration: chosen + supported (real n=939 fit,
promoted). P2 scattering-saturation: chosen + supported (concave 5/7 +
band 3/3 real). P3 state-space-fusion: deferred/candidate (in-silico
only — needs real drift). P4 spectral+coverage: candidate (4a selftest +
torun-adjacent; 4b design-layer). Never present P3/P4 as confirmed.
cards.front: The honest two-axis standing of the four pillars, right now?
cards.title: Honest standing

cards.back:
Mechanism: per-env ρ(count, CV) = +0.70…+1.00 in 7/7 real environments
across 2 platforms. Scale: platforms occupy separated CV bands
(meneghello ~0.4–0.5 vs WiMANS ~0.03–0.2); zero-shot LOEO MAE 1.75 vs
in-env oracle 0.72 vs predict-mean 2.07. The rank transfers; the absolute
mapping needs anchors.
cards.front:
"The mechanism travels, the scale does not" — give the concrete numbers
behind the slogan.
cards.title: What travels

cards.back:
Under repeated sampling, 95% of intervals constructed this way would
cover the true parameter. Misreading: "there is a 95% probability the
parameter is in THIS interval" — that is a credible-interval (Bayesian)
statement, not a frequentist CI.
cards.front:
What does a 95% confidence interval actually mean, and what is the
committee-bait misreading?
cards.title: Confidence intervals

cards.back:
Spearman correlates RANKS — robust to monotone nonlinearity and outliers,
right for small-n campaign reductions. But it saturates near 1 for ANY
monotone relation, so it is blind to effect MAGNITUDE — which is why the
band-ordering claim uses Cohen's d, not ρ.
cards.front:
When do we use Spearman ρ instead of Pearson r, and what is Spearman
blind to?
cards.title: Spearman vs Pearson

cards.back:
The standard equivalence test: declare equivalence iff BOTH one-sided
tests reject — the effect is significantly above −Δ AND below +Δ (i.e.
the CI falls inside the equivalence margin). Failing TOST means you
CANNOT claim equivalence; it does NOT prove a difference. The powered
drift-trigger replication failed TOST vs the oracle — so "≈ oracle" from
the pilot must not travel.
cards.front: What is TOST (two one-sided tests), and what does failing it mean?
cards.title: TOST

cards.back:
D = the maximum gap between two empirical CDFs; nonparametric test that
two samples come from one distribution. Trap: pooling links × seeds as
"observations" inflates n with non-independent points → over-powered
p-values. Cite the per-(link,seed) statistic, not the pooled one.
cards.front:
What does the two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test measure, and what
independence trap did our campaigns hit?
cards.title: KS test

cards.back:
Distribution-free finite-sample marginal coverage: calibrate the
nonconformity scores on held-out data and the resulting prediction
intervals contain the truth with probability ≥ 1−α, under exchangeability
— no Gaussian or model-correctness assumptions. Our conformal-count-
intervals hypothesis rides on the anchored/drift-weighted variant.
cards.front: What guarantee does conformal prediction give a count estimator?
cards.title: Conformal prediction

cards.back:
Nonparametric monotone-trend test on a time series (counts concordant vs
discordant pairs); no linearity or normality assumptions. Used for drift
claims: "does error trend upward over sessions" — paired with Sen's slope
for magnitude. One of the named sim_reduction_run reductions.
cards.front: Mann–Kendall test — what is it for and why do we use it?
cards.title: Mann–Kendall

cards.back:
d = (mean₁ − mean₂) / pooled SD — a standardised mean difference.
Conventionally 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. We report d when the
claim is about magnitude (band ordering 3/3 rooms; BLE presence
d = 2.3–3.7) and keep ρ for monotone association.
cards.front: Cohen's d — definition and the rough interpretation ladder?
cards.title: Effect sizes

cards.back:
A single seed is one draw from run-level randomness (placement, arrival,
channel noise) — its point estimate has unknown spread; T* was measured
seed-fragile ([0.25, 1.5, 0.25] m across seeds). House rule: multi-seed
runs reduced via multi_seed_ci (mean + CI over seeds); single-seed
numbers are labelled anecdotes.
cards.front:
Why does every simulation claim require multiple seeds, and what is the
house mechanism?
cards.title: Multiple seeds

choices: Session-fingerprint leakage — occupancy is confounded with session/day/channel, so the classifier identifies the recording session, not the occupancy
The features are excellent and the problem is solved
The dataset is unusually clean
AUC saturates at high n regardless of signal
cards.explanation:
persons=0/1/2 each map to distinct sessions (different days AND
channels), so file-level CV separates sessions perfectly. The mechanism
scalar showed NO 0-vs-1 difference (MWU p = 0.83). Perfect scores demand
a leakage audit before celebration.
cards.question:
The Zaman occupancy dataset gave AUC = 1.000 for EVERY feature family.
What is the correct diagnosis?
cards.title: Leakage

cards.back:
Leave-One-{Session, Room, Environment}-Out: hold out an entire group so
the test set shares no session/room/environment identity with training.
Random splits leak group fingerprints and overstate accuracy; the honest
generalisation number is the group-held-out one (our LOEO across 7 real
environments).
cards.front:
LOSO / LORO / LOEO — what are they and why do they matter more than
random splits?
cards.title: Cross-validation design

cards.back:
MI measures how much count information the feature carries independent of
any downstream model or threshold choice — comparable across sims and
datasets. OPERAnet real data: I(count; CSI-amp-variance) = 0.174 nats,
inside the sim's predicted 0.15–0.31 band; mean amplitude only 0.04.
cards.front:
Why report mutual information I(count; feature) in nats alongside
accuracy?
cards.title: Information-theoretic evaluation

cards.back:
The full Phase-4 analysis harness (4 calibration regimes, drift-slope
contrasts, LOSO/LORO, named baselines, and an explicit DEFEATER rule) was
written, self-tested, and locked BEFORE any hardware data exists — the
capture schema is defined by the analysis, so results cannot be
garden-of-forking-paths artefacts.
cards.front: What makes the IP-106 hardware protocol a genuine pre-registration?
cards.title: Pre-registration

choices: Predict-the-mean (2.07): zero-shot transfer barely beats knowing nothing, a +1.04-person penalty vs in-env oracle 0.72 — that gap IS the case for recalibration
A random classifier at 50%
Human annotator error
The state of the art from the literature
cards.explanation:
Named baselines (predict-mean, in-env oracle) bracket every reported
number in the cross-env study: 0.72 oracle < 1.32 two-anchor < 1.75
zero-shot < 2.07 predict-mean. Without the bracket, 1.75 means nothing.
cards.question: Which baseline turns "zero-shot MAE 1.75" from a number into a finding?
cards.title: Baselines

cards.back:
A hierarchical model where group parameters are drawn from a shared
prior: estimates shrink toward the population mean in proportion to their
uncertainty. Pillar 1 models per-environment calibration this way — the
measured "42% recovery with 2 anchors" is REPRODUCED as EB shrinkage
(posterior k=2 MAE 1.23 ≈ measured 1.32), so the empirical result becomes
a prediction of the theory.
cards.front:
What is partial pooling / empirical-Bayes shrinkage, and where does it
appear in the thesis?
cards.title: Partial pooling

cards.back:
Under a weak (flat) prior, extreme-spread D-optimal placement helps
(1.14 < 1.24 random); under the strong nested prior it INVERTS
(1.31 > 1.13) because it over-leverages noisy count tails. The correct
criterion is Bayesian-optimal design — maximise posterior information
GIVEN the prior. The hypothesis defeater was sharpened accordingly.
cards.front:
Frequentist D-optimal vs Bayesian-optimal anchor placement — which wins
and why?
cards.title: Optimal design

cards.back:
Coverage exhibits diminishing returns (adding a sensor helps less the
more you already have) = submodular set function; for monotone submodular
objectives greedy selection achieves ≥ (1 − 1/e) ≈ 63% of the optimum
(Nemhauser 1978). Verified 0 violations on our floor geometry; greedy hit
1.00 of optimal there. Counting-optimal ≠ coverage-optimal (Jaccard 0.50)
→ Pareto front.
cards.front:
Why does submodularity license greedy sensor placement, and with what
guarantee?
cards.title: Submodularity

cards.back:
NVIDIA's differentiable ray-tracing radio-propagation engine (part of the
Sionna link-level library): a 3D scene with material properties yields
per-path channels → CFR/CSI tensors. Our sionna-csi-runner wraps it:
scene + emitters + scatterers (agents as lossy primitives) → synthetic
CSI over time; CPU on CI, Apple Metal locally (~12× faster).
cards.front: What is Sionna RT and how do we use it?
cards.title: Sionna RT

cards.back:
walk-notebook (JuPedSim + agenda/FSM engine on a real floor bundle)
produces trajectories → sionna-csi-runner replays them as moving
scatterers over the ray-traced scene → links.parquet of per-link CSI
features + occupancy. One experiment, two physics engines, shared
geometry from PostGIS.
cards.front: Describe the coupled crowd→channel experiment chain.
cards.title: Coupled chain

choices: Structure and sensitivity evidence only — the noise model is self-authored, so sim cannot confirm its own absolute accuracy claims
Full empirical evidence, since the ray tracer solves Maxwell-accurate physics
No evidence value at all
Evidence for 2.4 GHz but not 5 GHz
cards.explanation:
The campaign-rigor audit's standing verdict: the sim corpus is
self-confirming for accuracy numbers. Sim results inform structure,
mechanisms, and sensitivity; accuracy claims need real data (OPERAnet,
WiMANS, first-party hardware).
cards.question: What epistemic status do our synthetic-CSI campaign results have?
cards.title: What sim may claim

cards.back:
OPERAnet exp028 (real Bristol capture, 6→1 people): CSI amplitude
variance steps down monotonically with count; I(count; variance) = 0.174
nats, CI [0.139, 0.208] — INSIDE the sim's predicted 0.15–0.31 band.
The sim is validated where it claims counting works, which makes its
walls-kill-counting negative a credible prediction rather than an
artefact.
cards.front: What is the one POSITIVE sim-to-real validation we hold, precisely?
cards.title: External validation

cards.back:
Synthetic 2-floor room-ID hits 0.99 vs 0.83 on real data: floor identity
is redundantly encoded (absolute level + spread + delay spread + K).
Neither feature-level impairments (even AGC σ16 dB → 0.866) nor
tensor-level CFO/STO/phase chains (→ 0.974) close the gap — no single
impairment dents it. Fix is scene/material DIVERSITY, not a post-hoc
noise knob (WiSegRT ablation predicts this).
cards.front:
What is the sim's known "over-coding" failure and why can't a noise layer
fix it?
cards.title: Over-coding

cards.back:
The absolute diffuse-power form (p_d0/γ) swamped the ray-traced channel
by ~80 dB — sim CSI became overlay-dominated and material/geometry drift
was byte-identical (inert). Fix: K_dB(N) = k0 − slope·N, with per-link
diffuse power = |H_det|²/K(N) — diffuse is now a bounded fraction of each
link's ray-traced power and inherits the scene physics.
cards.front:
Why was occupancy-diffuse power reparameterised to channel-relative
Rician K (IP-119)?
cards.title: Rician-K reparameterisation

cards.back:
Re-identification — re-fitting the drifted map against fresh anchors —
recovers most of the count-MAE penalty. Resetting to the original
calibration recovers almost none of it, at every cadence tested.
cards.front:
On the ray-traced material-drift sweep, what is the difference between
recalibration-as-RESET and recalibration-as-RE-IDENTIFICATION?
cards.title: Material drift result
cards.why:
Recalibration is not "restore the factory setting". It is a local re-fit,
and that distinction is what the whole calibration spine rests on.

cards.back:
Only when clutter intersects the link plane. Real-height furniture
(0.45–0.9 m) below a 2.4 m Tx / 1.2 m Rx plane is CSI-invisible (max
per-link Δ 0.08 dB); force footprints to 1.8 m → 9.17 dB; drop Rx to
0.6 m → 13.23 dB. Gate ≈ 100–165× either way. Bodies (1.7 m) span the
plane and own the channel; a furniture-blind CSI model is defensible in
this geometry — a furniture-blind WALKER model is not.
cards.front: When is furniture visible to CSI, per the furniture observatory?
cards.title: Furniture and the antenna plane

cards.back:
The busiest AND best-instrumented room read its own occupancy WORST
(corr −0.06; lowest amplitude variance = saturated), while a near-empty
room with one Rx read +0.53. Spearman(peak occupancy, observability)
= −0.70: busier rooms are LESS legible — dense hubs saturate under
constant occlusion. Caveat: observability was defined as LINEAR
correlation; near-zero ≠ no information.
cards.front: State the observability paradox found on ray-traced CSI.
cards.title: Observability paradox

cards.back:
Metal is ~12× faster but Float32-bound with path depth ≤ 4, and the Metal
PathSolver LOSES deep-shadow paths (~73 dB discrepancy vs llvm in deep
shadow) — fine for relative sweeps, not for absolute deep-null claims.
RadioMapSolver adds its own traps (sample cap, deterministic lattice —
fixed by rotation averaging).
cards.front: What are the Apple-Metal Sionna caveats that gate local runs?
cards.title: Metal backend caveats

cards.back:
A prompt-driven experiment brief (question, hypotheses, arms, success
criteria, budget) executed by a supervisor that fans out runs, reduces
them with named statistics, writes a synthesis, passes an adversarial
critic, and SEALS the session (immutable, ULID-identified, vault-synced).
Experiments are campaigns — not ad-hoc scripts.
cards.front: What is an IP-081 campaign, and what seals a session?
cards.title: Campaign system

cards.back:
No published comparison of Sionna-synthesized vs MEASURED indoor CSI
exists (confirmed by search) — the exact evidence a fidelity claim needs.
Honest positioning: our OPERAnet band-check is a feature-level
validation, not tensor-level fidelity; the impairment magnitudes (CFO
~200 Hz vs CARM's measured 80 kHz) are physically motivated but
uncalibrated.
cards.front:
What key piece of evidence is missing from the whole field of synthetic
CSI, and why does it matter to your defense?
cards.title: Fidelity gap

cards.back:
Four research questions, serving three objectives:
O1 — Calibration
O2 — Structure-grounded sensing
O3 — Generalisation and transfer
cards.example:
Asked "what is your second objective?", the answer is a title and a
register, not a paraphrase: "O2 — Structure-grounded sensing", served by RQ2, RQ3.

How many research questions does the thesis pose, and what are the
objectives they serve?
cards.title: How many, and what they serve

The count and the objective titles are declared once in the vault and
rendered into both the thesis and this deck, so the number you say aloud

To detect and model human movement in indoor environments using only the

cards.example:
The clause does real work, so watch it exclude things.

A phone app that reports its own location: **excluded** — the occupant is
carrying something and doing something. Turnstile counts: **excluded** at
the room scale, since they measure a boundary and not a space. A camera:
not excluded by this clause at all, and excluded elsewhere on privacy
grounds — which is worth knowing, because a committee that finds the goal
statement excluding cameras has found an overclaim.

Our own participant instrument looks like a violation and is not: it is a
paced emitter and a LABEL source used to build the reference, never the
deployed product. If the answer to "so people do have to carry a phone?"
is anything other than "only during calibration", the goal has been
misstated.

cards.front:
State the thesis's single overarching goal in one sentence, without naming
a technology.
cards.title: The one goal
cards.why:
"Without asking occupants to carry or do anything" is the load-bearing
clause. It is what rules out the device-based family the introduction
criticises, and it is why a device COUNT can only ever be a calibration
reference and never the product.

cards.back:
O1 — Calibration: a trustworthy reference and when to refresh it.
O2 — Structure-grounded sensing: how the environment shapes the signal
(the forward physics).
O3 — Generalisation and the simulation-to-real transfer: what decides
whether a model trained here works there.
cards.example:
The division is not thematic — it is a division of EVIDENCE, and that is
the answer to "why three?".

O1 cannot be settled in simulation, because a simulator cannot tell you
whether a real operator can obtain a trustworthy anchor. O2 and O3 cannot
be settled on our hardware, because we have one building and one chipset
family. So each objective is assigned to the evidence that can actually
close it: hardware for O1, geometry-faithful simulation and public
multi-environment corpora for O2 and O3.

If a committee asks "why not just measure everything yourselves?", that is
the answer: one building cannot answer a generalisation question, and a
simulator cannot answer a deployment one.

figures.caption: Each objective, the question it answers, and the evidence that can close it. The third column is why the objectives are separate at all.
rows: **can the reference be trusted, and when refreshed?**
how does the room shape the signal?
does a model trained here work there?

cards.front: Name O1, O2 and O3 in one phrase each.
cards.title: The three objectives
cards.why:
Each answers a different question about how such a system can be made to
work and to KEEP working. O1 is the deployment contribution and must be
settled on hardware; O2 and O3 are settled in geometry-faithful simulation
and on public corpora.

choices: The evaluation chapter, since it holds the numbers.
The CSI-sensing chapter.
The BLE-augmentation chapter.
The crowd-modelling chapter.
cards.example:
The rule generalises, and stating it beats memorising four rows: **a
question is answered where its argument lives, not where its numbers
live.**

So when a committee member holds up a table from the evaluation chapter and
asks "is this your answer to RQ2?", the first sentence is: "that is the
evidence; the answer is developed in the CSI-sensing chapter, and this
table is what it rests on." RQ4 is the single exception, and knowing WHY it
is an exception — a policy is a measurement, not an argument — is worth more
than knowing that it is one.
cards.explanation:
RQ2 is answered in the CSI-sensing chapter, and it serves objectives O2
and O3. The first option is the trap and it is a good one: the evaluation
chapter holds the numbers, but a research question is answered where its
argument is developed, not where its evidence is tabulated. RQ1 goes to
BLE augmentation, RQ3 to crowd modelling, RQ4 to evaluation — and RQ4 is
the only one whose answering chapter IS the evaluation chapter, because
the recalibration policy is a measurement rather than an argument.

figures.caption: The routing, with the exception marked. Every row but the last answers its question where the argument is built; RQ4's answer IS a measurement.

types and band survive a change, and how accuracy degrades over time?
cards.title: RQ to chapter

cards.back:
Both serve O1, calibration. RQ1 asks whether a device-count reference can
be good enough to anchor a CSI model; RQ4 asks what policy keeps that
anchoring worth its cost over time.
cards.example:
Buying a set of kitchen scales and then living with them. RQ1 is "is this
scale accurate enough to trust?". RQ4 is "how often must I re-check it
against a known weight, and what error am I accepting between checks?".

The pairing is why a committee question about calibration frequency is not
a question about hardware quality, and vice versa. A perfectly trustworthy
anchor that must be re-collected every hour is not deployable; a cheap
anchor that holds for a month may be. Answering the wrong half of O1 is
one of the easiest mistakes to make under pressure, because both halves use
the word "calibration".

figures.caption: O1 has two halves and each has its own question. RQ1 establishes the anchor; RQ4 decides when to spend it. Both need hardware, which is why both carry pre-registered rather than delivered legs.

cards.front: RQ1 and RQ4 both serve which objective? What does that pairing mean?
cards.title: Which objective a question serves
cards.why:
They are the two halves of the deployment contribution: can the anchor be
trusted, and when should it be spent. Neither can be settled in
simulation, which is why both have hardware legs that are pre-registered
rather than delivered.

cards.back:
Tier one — re-analysis of public multi-environment CSI corpora, which
delivers the cross-environment calibration results.
Tier two — characterisation of the deployed instrument, which delivers the
bounds every later occupancy claim must be read against.
Tier three — the pre-registered in-vivo campaign, whose protocol is frozen
and whose result slots are labelled and empty.
cards.example:
The hostile version of the question is "so you have no occupancy results",
and the tiers are what turn that into a two-sentence answer instead of a
concession.

"Tier one is measured, on public corpora, and it is where the
cross-environment calibration result comes from. Tier two is measured, on
our own fleet, and it is why you can read any later occupancy number at
all — it is where the delivery spread and the fault classes are
characterised. Tier three is frozen and empty, deliberately, and the
protocol was registered before the room was booked."

An empty result slot with a frozen protocol is a stronger position than a
filled one with a protocol written afterwards, and saying so first is
better than being led to it.

figures.caption: The three tiers, their status, and what each delivers. The status column is the one to have cold: two measured, one frozen and empty.
rows: the bounds later claims are read against

cards.front:
Name the three evidence tiers of the evaluation chapter and say what each
delivers.
cards.title: The three evidence tiers
cards.why:
The chapter separates what is measured from what is planned BECAUSE the
credibility of the eventual occupancy results depends on that separation
being visible now. The eventual numbers should inherit the credibility of
the design rather than borrow it.

choices: They are the same three things under two names.
Tier one is stage two executed; tier two is the instrument half of stage three executed; tier three is the occupancy half of stage three, pending.
Tier one is stage one, tier two is stage two, tier three is stage three.
The tiers describe the chapters and the stages describe the campaigns; there is no mapping.
cards.example:
Why the mismatch exists is the interesting part, and it is a decision
rather than an accident.

A STAGE is a kind of data. A TIER is a kind of claim. Synthetic data is a
whole stage and delivers no evidence tier, because its role is to
stress-test components — you cannot cite a simulation as a measurement of a
building. And one stage, first-party, splits across two tiers because half
of it is done and half of it is not: the instrument is characterised, the
occupancy campaign is frozen.

So the sentence to have ready is: "stages are data, tiers are claims, and
they do not line up because synthetic data supports no claim of its own and
our first-party work is half finished."
cards.explanation:
The mapping is deliberately not one-to-one, and knowing that is the point
of the card. Stage one — fully synthetic JuPedSim-to-Sionna work — is
reported in the modelling chapters rather than as an evidence tier,
because it stress-tests components rather than delivering results. Stage
three splits: the instrument half is executed and is tier two, the
occupancy half is pre-registered and is tier three. That split is the
single most important structural fact about the evaluation chapter.

figures.caption: Stages are kinds of DATA, tiers are kinds of CLAIM. Stage one supports no tier; stage three splits across two. That mismatch is the structural fact, not a bookkeeping error.

nodes.label: reported in the modelling chapters — no tier

cards.question:
How do the three evidence TIERS map onto the three methodological STAGES
(synthetic, public real, first-party)?
cards.title: Tiers versus stages

cards.back:
Pillar 1 — hierarchical calibration (partial pooling).
Pillar 2 — the scattering link (a derived concave, saturating law), with
Pillar 2a its spectral reading via random-matrix theory.
Pillar 3 — state-space fusion (one filter, two readouts).
Pillar 4 — spectral count plus submodular coverage.
cards.example:
Recite them as a pipeline for one measurement, not as a list, and the order
stops being arbitrary.

A room's signal variability arrives. **Pillar 2** says what that
variability means in terms of a number of movers, and that the relation is
concave and saturating rather than linear. **Pillar 1** says how to
re-parameterise that relation for THIS room from two anchors. **Pillar 3**
says how to carry the estimate forward in time between anchorings, and when
to demand a new one. **Pillar 4** handles the two cases the first three
cannot: a crowd that is sitting still, and where to put the receivers in
the first place.

A committee asking "why four?" is asking whether any of them is decoration.
The pipeline answer names a job each one does that no other one does.

figures.caption: The four pillars as one pipeline over a single measurement. Pillar 4 is drawn to the side because it acts before and beneath the others — it decides where the receivers were, and rescues the still-crowd case.

nodes.label:
P3 — state-space fusion
carry forward, retrigger

cards.front: Name the four pillars in order, one phrase each.
cards.title: The four pillars
cards.why:
Their through-line is one sentence: a single scattering-derived link,
reparameterised per environment by a hierarchical calibration model,
tracked over time by a state-space filter, with the two hard cases — still
crowds and sensor placement — handled by spectral and submodular
arguments.

cards.back:
The hypotheses are the EMPIRICAL contract: each is a measurable claim
paired with a refutation condition. Taken singly they are a set of
measurements. The pillars are the THEORETICAL contribution those
measurements instantiate — four formal models, each unifying several
hypotheses and each predicting something testable.
cards.example:
The 42% recovery figure is the whole argument in one number, so use it.

As a **hypothesis result** it says: two anchors recovered 42% of the
transfer gap in our corpus. True, checkable, and unable to tell you what
happens with three anchors, or in a building unlike ours.

As a **pillar prediction** it says: shrinkage towards a population prior
has a closed form, that form predicts roughly this much recovery from two
anchors, and here is the measurement agreeing with it. Now the number
generalises — you can ask the model what four anchors would buy, and be
wrong in a way that is diagnosable.

A measurement that agrees with a mechanism is worth more than the same
measurement alone, and the gap between those two sentences is what the
pillars are for.

figures.caption: The same finding under both contracts. The right-hand column is what a doctoral contribution adds to a competent measurement.

cards.front:
What is the difference between the hypotheses and the pillars? Why does
the thesis need both?
cards.title: Empirical versus theoretical contract
cards.why:
The pillars exist because a competent measurement study is not a doctoral
contribution. Their job is to turn "we observed 42 per cent recovery" into
"the model says two anchors must recover about this much, and they do."

choices: All four are chosen and supported.
Pillars 1 and 2 are chosen and supported on real public data; Pillars 3 and 4 are candidates whose decisive tests are reserved for first-party hardware.
Pillars 1 and 3 are supported; Pillars 2 and 4 are candidates.
Only Pillar 1 is supported; the rest are speculative.
cards.example:
Volunteering the ordering is stronger than defending it, and there is a
form of words for that.

"Two of the four are supported on real public data. Pillar 3's evidence is
in-silico, with the powered replication's demotions already applied —
including one correlation whose interval widened enough that I report the
demoted number rather than the pilot's. Pillar 4 is confirmed in simulation
and, for the seated count, on one paper's real hardware."

Notice what that sentence does: it names the weakness, names the specific
demotion, and gives the committee nothing to catch you with. The answer
"all four are supported" is not merely wrong — it invites exactly the audit
that finds the in-silico evidence.
cards.explanation:
Pillar 1 is fitted on the real pooled corpus, and Pillar 2's concave law
is AIC-preferred over a line in most counting-band environments — both
chosen and supported. Pillar 3's fusion-and-trigger evidence is in-silico
with the powered replication's demotions applied, and Pillar 4's mechanism
is confirmed in simulation plus, for the seated count, on one paper's real
hardware. The thesis states this ordering explicitly so that the
theoretical ambition never outruns the evidence — and answering "all four"
is exactly the overreach it is guarding against.

figures.caption: Where each pillar's evidence comes from, and what that licenses. The last column is the honest verb for each row.
rows: fitted on the real pooled corpus
AIC-preferred over a line in most environments

cards.question:
Which pillars are chosen-and-supported on real public data, and which
remain candidates?
cards.title: Which pillar is weakest

cards.back:
The refuted continuity prior is stated in the objectives chapter as a
retired hypothesis, developed in the crowd-modelling chapter, and
re-reported in the fusion chapter. The certified-empty false-trigger
constraint sits in the fusion chapter and in the evaluation's tier two.
The delay-spread band contrast that died under re-reduction is named in
the conclusion's contribution list.
cards.example:
A negative appears in three places for three different reasons, and knowing
which place a question is aimed at saves an answer from wandering.

The **objectives chapter** records that the claim was made and retired —
that is the honesty ledger. The **crowd-modelling chapter** develops why it
failed: the velocity field indoors is nearly unobservable, so the
divergence term is inert. The **fusion chapter** records the consequence:
the temporal mechanism moved to the state-space filter.

So "where is your refuted hypothesis?" has three correct answers and they
are not interchangeable. Claim, mechanism, consequence.

figures.caption: Three negatives, and where each is stated, developed and consumed. Each row is a design the field no longer has to spend a year on.

cards.front:
Where in the document are the documented negatives stated, and which are
they?
cards.title: Where the negatives live
cards.why:
All three are counted as CONTRIBUTIONS, not as absences, because each
retires a design the field would otherwise keep proposing.

cards.back:
It documents the substrate, the synthetic-data platform, the datasets and
the testbed so a third party can reproduce the work. It PROVES NO
HYPOTHESIS — it says so in its own first line.
cards.example:
The test of whether something belongs in the appendix is a question about
its role, not about its length.

"The fleet runs Ubuntu 24.04 with a patched driver" is appendix material:
needed to reproduce, proves nothing. "Two receivers on the same channel
disagree by 11.6 points of delivered fraction" is NOT appendix material,
even though it is about the instrument — it is a finding, it bounds later
claims, and it lives in the implementation chapter with the evaluation
consuming it.

The failure this rule prevents is a familiar one: an appendix that quietly
accumulates results nobody has to defend, because nobody reads an appendix
adversarially.

figures.caption: Two facts about the same instrument, sorted by role. The test is whether anything later depends on it, not whether it is technical.
rows: OS, driver version, image build path

cards.front: What is the supporting appendix for, and what does it explicitly NOT do?
cards.title: The supporting appendix
cards.why:
It exists to pay for the reproducibility commitment the evaluation chapter
makes on the thesis's behalf. It also holds the notation table and the
privacy and ethics posture, which are prerequisites rather than paperwork.

choices: The evaluation chapter owns it; the implementation chapter consumes it.
The implementation chapter owns it; the evaluation chapter consumes it as a tier-two bound.
The CSI-sensing chapter owns it; nothing consumes it.
The supporting appendix owns it; the conclusion consumes it.
cards.example:
Say the dependency out loud and the two chapters stop looking like
duplicates: **the instrument chapter measures the instrument; the
evaluation chapter measures the world THROUGH it.**

So the 11.6-point spread is owned where it was measured, and it appears in
the evaluation as a bound — the reason a single-receiver occupancy number
from this fleet cannot be quoted without saying which receiver. The same
applies to the yield census: the implementation chapter owns the finding
that 15–16% of delivered records are all-zero, and the evaluation chapter
is where that becomes "quote 83%, not 98.4%".
cards.explanation:
The full account — fleet description, gate audit, rate ladder, fault-class
forensics — is in the implementation chapter, which is titled "The
Measurement Instrument" precisely because instrument characterisation is
its subject. The evaluation chapter's tier two CONSUMES those results as
bounds that govern how every later occupancy claim must be read. Knowing
which way that dependency points is the difference between a chapter and a
duplicate.

figures.caption: The dependency has one direction. Instrument results flow into the evaluation as bounds; nothing flows back. A chapter that consumed its own bounds would be a duplicate.

nodes.label: delivery spread · yield census · fault classes
every later occupancy claim, read against those bounds

cards.question:
A committee member asks about the 11.6-point inter-receiver delivery
spread. Which chapter owns that result, and which chapter consumes it?
cards.title: Where the instrument is described

cards.back:
Introduction; State of the Art; Objectives, Hypotheses and the Output
Contract; System Design; CSI-Based Sensing; BLE and Device-Activity
Augmentation; Indoor Crowd Modelling; Calibration and Fusion; The
Measurement Instrument; Evaluation; Conclusion. Then Supporting Material
as an appendix.
cards.example:
A committee reads the table of contents before it reads anything else, and
the third chapter is what it notices.

In the ordinary shape, objectives are a section of the introduction and
hypotheses appear wherever they are tested. That shape lets a claim be
written after its evidence — which is not dishonest, and is unfalsifiable.
Promoting them to their own chapter, before any system exists, means every
later chapter can be checked against a commitment that was made earlier in
the same document.

So the answer to "why is chapter three a chapter?" is: because it is the
contract, and a contract signed after delivery is not one.

figures.caption: The eleven, grouped by what they do. The third block is the unusual one, and it is the only one that has to come before the system exists.
rows: **what is claimed, before anything is built**
System Design · CSI Sensing · BLE Augmentation · Crowd Modelling · Calibration and Fusion

cards.front: Name the eleven chapters in order.
cards.title: The chapter order
cards.why:
The unusual one is the third. Stating objectives, hypotheses and the
output contract as their OWN chapter, after the literature and before any
system is built, is what makes the rest of the document a contract rather
than a narrative.

choices: Because it is a metric choice, and metrics belong with objectives.
Because it determines what every subsequent claim is a claim ABOUT, so it has to be settled before any of them are made.
Because the evaluation chapter was written last.
Because conformal prediction is a theoretical result rather than an empirical one.
cards.example:
Consider what would happen if the contract were fixed in the evaluation
chapter instead. Every earlier chapter would have been written against an
undecided output, so its claims would have to be re-read once the contract
arrived — and any claim that turned out to be about a point estimate would
quietly become a claim about a distribution.

The concrete symptom of getting this wrong is a thesis that reports MAE
everywhere and adds calibration metrics at the end. Ours reports the band
and the calibration wherever it reports a count, because the contract said
so before the first count was computed.
cards.explanation:
It is stated before any hypothesis, and the chapter says why: the contract
decides what the system's output IS, so it decides what everything after
it is claiming. The consequence runs through the whole thesis — where a
later chapter reports a count it also reports the band and the calibration
of its stated confidence, and the evaluation chapter scores CONTRACTS
rather than only point error.
cards.question:
Why is the output contract fixed in the objectives chapter rather than in
the evaluation chapter?
cards.title: Where the output contract is fixed

cards.back:
It is the absence of a first-party capture WITH A KNOWN NUMBER OF PEOPLE
IN THE ROOM. It is NOT the absence of first-party capture — the deployment
has produced a twelve-hour drift baseline, a paired-band delivery
contrast, a rate ladder, a nine-observer coordinated walk and a device
census over the accumulated archive.
cards.example:
The difference between the two framings is the difference between a project
that is behind and a project that has one experiment left.

Wrong framing: "we have no real data." The fleet has produced a twelve-hour
drift baseline, a paired-band contrast, a rate ladder, a nine-observer
coordinated walk and a device census — that is a great deal of real data.

Right framing: "every occupancy we have certified is zero." One number is
missing from an otherwise populated table, and the protocol for obtaining
it is frozen and pre-registered. That is a gap you can close in one
campaign, and saying it that precisely is what makes the answer sound like
a plan instead of an apology.

figures.caption: What the deployment has measured, and the one column that is empty. Naming the gap this narrowly is what makes it a plan rather than an apology.
rows: **Capture with a known number of people in the room**

cards.front:
The thesis names its weakest link precisely. What is it, and what is it
NOT?
cards.title: The weakest link
cards.why:
Every occupancy this deployment has certified so far is zero. Everything
the calibration spine claims is a claim about how a signal responds to
occupancy, so that is what keeps the spine at plausible rather than
measured. Naming the gap this narrowly is what makes it actionable.

cards.back:
It is a living hypothesis in the O1 calibration spine — "recalibration is
a double-edged asset" — and it recurs in future work.
cards.example:
The fork has a testable hinge, which is what stops it being an ethics
paragraph.

An unauthorised observer can obtain the ENVIRONMENT-level shift for free —
they can stand outside the room and watch the furniture change. What they
cannot obtain is an ENCODING-level anchor: a labelled count from inside the
room, on the operator's hardware. And the encoding axis is precisely the
one where transfer degrades most.

So the empirical question is whether the accuracy recalibration buys is
carried by the axis the attacker can reach or the axis they cannot. If it
is the second, then the entitlement to anchors is itself the defence — and
that is a result, not a reassurance.

figures.caption: The fork, as two mechanistic arms with one testable hinge. Which arm is true is an empirical question about which shift axis carries the gain.
rows: can obtain that shift for free

cards.front:
Where does the dual-use question live, and what makes it a genuine fork
rather than a caveat?
cards.title: Ownership of the dual-use question
cards.why:
It is a fork because BOTH arms are mechanistic. If a channel-shift
correction contains no term for authorisation, the headline contribution
is also an attack enabler. But if what carries the operator's accuracy is
the ENTITLEMENT to trustworthy anchors, recalibration is a de-facto
defence. The thesis reports whichever it finds, and either resolution is a
result.

choices: Both say it belongs to the CSI chapter; the role is a finer sub-category.
The tag says what the paper is ABOUT; the role says what it HOLDS UP. They are independent, and only the first is derivable from the abstract.
The tag was assigned by hand and the role by the taxonomy agent.
The role supersedes the tag once a paper is cited.
cards.example:
One paper, two orthogonal facts about it.

A survey of CSI crowd counting is ABOUT CSI sensing — any reader of its
abstract will say so, and a classifier will agree. What it HOLDS UP in this
thesis might be a `negative-target`: it is the practice the thesis argues
against, and the argument needs it to exist and be citable.

Now the operational consequence. If a chapter's citations look thin, no
amount of re-running the topical classifier will help, because the
classifier is not wrong — it is answering a different question. The fix is
to assign roles, which requires reading the paper's position relative to
the argument rather than its abstract.
cards.explanation:
Topical is not argumentative. The chapter tag answers "what is this
about?" and a taxonomy agent assigns it from the paper's own abstract. The
role answers "what does this hold up?" and can only be derived from the
paper's position relative to the thesis's argument. That is also why you
cannot recover argumentative weight by reclassifying: a topical classifier
re-reading the same abstract reaches the same correct topical conclusion.

figures.caption: Two axes, two provenances. The bottom-right cell is the one that cannot be automated from an abstract, which is why roles are curated.

cards.question:
A paper carries the tag `thesis/csi-sensing` and the argument role
`negative-target`. What do those two say?
cards.title: What a chapter tag is not

cards.back:
The objectives chapter's hypothesis table, for what was claimed and where
each claim now stands. Then the evaluation chapter's tier one, for what
has actually been measured on real data. Then the conclusion's
limitations, for what the author already knows is wrong with it.
cards.example:
Watch what each of the other orders does.

Evidence first invites "which claim was this supposed to support?" — the
reader has to reverse-engineer the contract, and will suspect it was
written afterwards. Limitations first reads as pre-emptive apology.
Claims first, evidence second, honesty third is the only order in which
each section answers a question the previous one raised.

It is also the order you can offer in one sentence at the start of a
defense, which converts an hour of being examined into an hour of being
followed.
