cards.front:
A reader has one hour and wants to know whether the thesis is any good.
Which three sections do you send them to, and in what order?
cards.title: Reading order for a stranger
cards.why:
That order tests the thesis on its own terms — claims first, evidence
second, honesty third — and it is the order a hostile reader would
construct anyway. Offering it yourself is a stronger position than being
led through it.

cards.back:
The sensor is privacy-preserving in what it RELEASES — an aggregate count
discloses far less than camera imagery — while the channel it reads can be
observed passively, through walls, and without the awareness of the people
being counted.
cards.example:
The two halves are easy to hold apart with one comparison.

What is RELEASED: "fourteen people in this room". A camera frame in the
same room releases faces, clothing, who is sitting with whom, and what is
on the screens. The count is genuinely the smaller disclosure, and that is
a real design achievement.

What is READ: a channel that passes through walls, from an emitter nobody
consented to, measurable by anyone with a compatible receiver and no line
of sight. That is a LARGER capability than a camera in one specific
respect — a camera cannot see through a wall, and a camera is visible.

Which is why the posture is engineered: a posted notice, a stated
data-handling policy, identifier randomisation. The modality does not grant
privacy; the deployment has to.

figures.caption: Released against read. Both columns are true at once, and answering with only the left one is the overclaim the thesis is written to avoid.

cards.front:
The introduction makes one caveat about privacy and honours it throughout.
What is it?
cards.title: The privacy caveat
cards.why:
So privacy is treated as a property to be ENGINEERED AND AUDITED — an
explicit consent, data-handling and identifier-randomisation posture in
the supporting appendix — rather than as something the modality grants by
construction. Claiming the modality is inherently private is the answer
the thesis is written to avoid.

choices: Nothing — tier three of the architecture was removed.
The field-valued estimation TARGET: a density field rather than a per-agent roster. Not a hard constraint.
A learned fundamental diagram that replaces the fixed parametric one.
The velocity field, which the state-space filter now estimates directly.
cards.example:
Two roles, one demoted and one intact, and the distinction is worth saying
precisely because the refutation looks larger than it was.

The **demoted** role: a conservation law as a PRIOR, penalising density
fields that fail to conserve mass. That was tested and retired — swapping
in an anti-physical version changed nothing.

The **intact** role: the continuum framing as a TARGET, which says that
what a radio can recover from a room is a density field and not a roster of
individuals. Nothing about the refutation touched that, and it is what
keeps the output contract distributional rather than per-person.

A committee asking "so why is there still a crowd-modelling chapter?" is
asking about the second role. The answer is that it decides what the system
is trying to estimate — which is a larger contribution than a
regularisation term would have been.
cards.explanation:
The continuum framing earns its place by fixing WHAT is estimated, and
that survived the refutation untouched: at indoor pedestrian densities and
room-scale resolutions, aggregate flux rather than individual paths is
what a radio can hope to recover. What was demoted is the stronger role —
a conservation-law prior regularising the inference. The load-bearing
temporal mechanism moved to the state-space filter of the fusion chapter.

figures.caption: What the refutation took and what it left. The surviving row is the larger of the two, which is why the chapter stayed.
rows: the physics term retired; smoothing beat every variant

TOST requires normality, which CSI data violates
TOST is only valid for paired samples
Nothing — TOST tests differences

The hybrid-fusion argument chain still misquotes TOST (open audit

From amplitude PHASE — amplitude itself is uninformative
From RSSI averaged over frames
No correction needed

Counting rides on second-order temporal statistics; absolute amplitude

choices: WiSegRT's Rx grid sat ~20 cm from clutter; with ceiling-AP/waist-Rx geometry, real-height furniture is measured CSI-invisible (max 0.08 dB) — the gate is link-plane ∩ clutter-height, confirmed from both directions at ~100–165×
WiSegRT was simulation-only, so it can be ignored
Our model does include furniture, so the premise is wrong
Furniture only matters at 2.4 GHz

The axis matters: forcing footprints to 1.8 m gives 9.17 dB; dropping Rx
to 0.6 m gives 13.23 dB. Same furniture, different antenna plane. A

The ray tracer solves real physics, so sim results are real results
All sensing papers do this, so it is accepted practice
The critic agent already validates every campaign

cards.title: The one-week story

cards.back:
The complex frequency response H(f) of the radio channel, estimated per
OFDM subcarrier (amplitude + phase per tone, per Tx-Rx antenna pair) from
the known preamble of each received frame. It describes how the environment
transformed the transmitted signal.
cards.front: What is Channel State Information (CSI) in Wi-Fi?
cards.title: What CSI is
cards.why: The opening definition — say it in one breath.

cards.back:
RSSI is one scalar per frame (total received power). CSI resolves the
channel per subcarrier and per antenna pair, so it preserves frequency
selectivity and phase — small path changes reshape the CSI pattern even
when total power (RSSI) barely moves.
cards.front: Why is CSI a richer sensing observable than RSSI?
cards.title: CSI vs RSSI

cards.back:
Indoors the signal arrives as a sum of paths (direct, reflected,
scattered). A body blocks, reflects, and scatters individual paths;
because CSI resolves the channel finely, these per-path perturbations
shift the amplitude/phase pattern measurably.
cards.front: Why does indoor multipath make CSI sensitive to human presence?
cards.title: Multipath
cards.why: The first-principles opener a committee uses to test depth vs. recitation.

cards.back:
Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiplexing splits the band into many
narrow orthogonal subcarriers. Equalising them requires estimating the
per-subcarrier channel from known pilots/preamble — that estimate IS the
CSI; sensing reuses what communication must compute anyway.
cards.front: What is OFDM and why does it give us CSI "for free"?
cards.title: OFDM

cards.back:
Rayleigh: no dominant path, the channel is a sum of many comparable
scattered components (magnitude Rayleigh-distributed). Rician: one
dominant (usually LoS) path plus diffuse scatter; the K-factor is the
ratio of dominant to diffuse power. K → 0 recovers Rayleigh.
cards.front: Rayleigh vs Rician fading — when does each apply?
cards.title: Fading models

cards.back:
K = deterministic (dominant-path) power / diffuse (scattered) power.
People add scatterers and block dominant paths, so K tends to fall as
occupancy rises — the diffuse fraction of the channel is where the crowd
signature lives.
cards.front:
What does the Rician K-factor measure, and why does it matter for crowd
sensing?
cards.title: Rician K

cards.back:
Motion changes path lengths over time; each moving scatterer modulates the
channel at a rate set by its radial velocity relative to the path
geometry. Indoor human motion lives at low Doppler frequencies — well
under ~300 Hz at Wi-Fi bands (CARM); walking is tens of Hz.
cards.front:
What creates the Doppler signature in Wi-Fi sensing, and roughly where
does indoor human motion sit spectrally?
cards.title: Doppler

cards.back:
v_max = λ · PRR / 4 — the packet-rate PRR bounds the fastest motion whose
Doppler you can sample unaliased (λ ≈ 5.6 cm at 5.3 GHz). Reported by
Ropitault et al. 2024 and Wang et al. 2022 — NOT by the qualitative-Doppler
papers (ma2020, chen2023, du2025).
cards.front:
What is the maximum trackable speed relation for CSI packet-rate sensing,
and who reports it?
cards.title: Speed–sampling relation
cards.why: Known citation trap — the formula is real, the usual citation is wrong.

cards.back:
PL(d) = PL(d0) + 10·n·log10(d/d0) + X, with path-loss exponent n (~2 free
space, 2–4+ indoors) and shadowing term X. It predicts mean received power
vs distance; fading rides on top of it.
cards.front: What is the log-distance path-loss model?
cards.title: Path loss

cards.back:
Coherence time: how long the channel stays effectively constant (set by
Doppler spread) — bounds the useful sampling interval. Coherence
bandwidth: over what frequency span the channel is flat (set by delay
spread) — determines how many independent subcarrier looks you get.
cards.front:
Coherence time and coherence bandwidth — what do they tell a sensing
system designer?
cards.title: Coherence

cards.explanation:
HT20 uses 56 usable tones (52 data + 4 pilots) out of a 64-point FFT;
legacy (a/g) OFDM uses 52; 242 is the 20 MHz resource-unit tone count in
802.11ax (HE). Our AX210 fleet observes 52- and 56-tone frames interleaved
on an ambient channel.
cards.question:
A 20 MHz 802.11n (HT) transmission delivers CSI on how many usable
subcarriers?
cards.title: Subcarrier counts

choices: Shorter wavelength: each mover perturbs the phasor sum by a larger fraction of λ, so per-mover fluctuation magnitude is larger
5 GHz has more subcarriers, so more information is always captured
2.4 GHz is absorbed by water and people are mostly water
5 GHz propagates further indoors, illuminating more of the room
cards.explanation:
The scattering-saturation pillar treats the band ordering as a wavelength
prediction about fluctuation magnitude per mover — confirmed on WiMANS by
Cohen's d in 3/3 rooms (measure magnitude with d, not Spearman ρ, which
saturates for any monotone relation).
cards.question:
Why does 5 GHz beat 2.4 GHz for crowd-counting discriminability in our
framework?
cards.title: Bands

cards.back:
The power-weighted spread of path arrival times from the channel impulse
response. Practical traps: window the CFR (e.g. Hann) before the IFFT or
sinc sidelobes read as fake multipath, and threshold taps (~−20 dB) or you
measure the noise floor.
cards.front: What is RMS delay spread and what practical trap does measuring it hide?
cards.title: Delay spread

cards.back:
The first body changes the channel a lot (large marginal effect); each
additional body adds a diminishing perturbation as the diffuse field
saturates. Our scattering law derives this: variance grows concavely with
count, Var ≈ σ²(1 − e^(−K/K0)), so the count signal compresses at high
occupancy.
cards.front: Why is detecting presence easy but counting hard in CSI sensing?
cards.title: Presence vs counting

cards.back:
The Wi-Fi Sensing amendment: standardises sensing measurement setup,
scheduling, and CSI-style feedback so sensing no longer depends on
vendor-specific CSI extraction hacks. Relevant as the "this will be
mainstream" framing for the thesis motivation.
cards.front: What is IEEE 802.11bf?
cards.title: Sensing standardisation

choices: Temporal variance of amplitude
Mean amplitude
Phase intercept
RSSI
cards.explanation:
Counting rides on amplitude VARIANCE, not mean: on OPERAnet exp028 the
variance carries I = 0.174 nats about count while mean amplitude carries
only 0.04 nats. Mean-level features are also destroyed by AGC on real
NICs.
cards.question:
Which CSI-derived statistic carries the crowd-count signal in both our
simulations and the OPERAnet real-data validation?
cards.title: The observable

cards.back:
Intel 5300 CSI Tool (legacy), Atheros CSI Tool, Nexmon (Broadcom, e.g.
Raspberry Pi), PicoScenes (SDR + multi-NIC), FeitCSI / iwlwifi vendor
path (Intel AX2xx). Our fleet: Intel AX210 on Raspberry Pi 5 via the
iax/iwlwifi vendor-command path, consumed by our own Rust daemon csid.
cards.front: Name the main CSI extraction toolchains and where our stack sits.
cards.title: Extraction toolchains

cards.back:
Raw per-packet phase is scrambled by CFO/SFO offsets (uniform-random
intercepts). Dividing CSI of two RX chains on the same NIC cancels the
common oscillator terms. Measured on our AX210 link: raw phase intercept
std 3.5 rad → ratio phase circular std 0.26 rad; amplitude CV 0.32 → 0.20.
Two active RX chains are therefore a hard capture requirement.
cards.front:
Why is the CSI ratio (two-antenna quotient) the primary observable on
commodity NICs?
cards.title: Why the ratio

cards.back:
The pair (ntone, modulation) of a CSI record. An ambient channel
interleaves unlike frames packet-by-packet (measured: 74% legacy-52 +
26% HT-56 on ch11), so mixing classes compares incompatible tone grids.
Every csiscope/IP-121 analytical view is scoped to one class.
cards.front:
What is a "record class" in our capture stack and why does every
analytical view scope to one?
cards.title: Record classes

cards.back:
(1) Storage is chain-major (contiguous ntone blocks per RX/TX chain), not
tone-interleaved. (2) Each coefficient stores the imaginary part first;
reading real-first yields i·conj(H) — amplitudes unchanged, every phase
mirrored. Decided by CIR causality: correct order gives early/late tap
energy ratio 21.3; swapped gives 0.48 (anti-causal, impossible).
cards.front:
The two silent CSI-layout bugs found in our capture stack — what were
they, and what test decided the byte order?
cards.title: Silent layout bug
cards.why: A committee-grade story about verifying your own pipeline.

cards.back:
Ambient/hostapd multicast is bursty (no ACK/retry; DTIM/queue bunching:
gap p50 15 ms vs commanded 40 ms, CV 2.6, 12% of wall time in >1 s
stalls) — inter-arrival is Erlang-like, not a clean sampling clock. Answer:
a paced monitor-mode injector in csid (absolute-deadline pacing, missed
slots skipped) or a unicast stream.
cards.front:
Why does passive ambient traffic fail as a Doppler-grade sampling source,
and what is our answer?
cards.title: Illuminator

choices: Source MAC sentinel ef:be:ad:de:ad:de (driver-side 0xdeadbeef fill)
By the AP's real MAC address
By a custom vendor IE in the beacon
By their fixed 56-tone HT format
cards.explanation:
Broadcast data frames without a station context get the deadbeef fill
pattern as smac; the AP's real MAC appears only on beacons. Filter on the
sentinel, not the AP MAC. (They are 52-tone legacy frames, not HT-56.)
cards.question: How are our illuminator frames identified in captures?
cards.title: Sentinel MAC

cards.back:
(1) The reported value is a positive magnitude — the dBm value is its
negative (valid range −18..−89 dBm). (2) −127 dBm is a firmware
"no measurement" sentinel, and that chain's CSI block is then a stale
duplicate (exact biconditional over 44k records). (3) Ambient vs
illuminated frames make RSSI bimodal — scope by source MAC.
cards.front: Three iax/AX210 RSSI facts every analysis must respect?
cards.title: RSSI semantics

cards.back:
Above roughly 80 °C the Pi 5 firmware throttles the ARM clock while
cpufreq keeps reporting the nominal frequency. The only truth is
`get_throttled` — its live bits and its sticky bits.
cards.front:
A fanless fleet node reports a healthy performance governor at 2.4 GHz.
Why is that not evidence it is running at full speed?
cards.title: Fleet thermals
cards.why:
The hottest fanless node idles in the low eighties, a few degrees under
the hard limit, so this is not a hypothetical. A node that looks healthy
in every governor reading can be silently cooked, and the fan is what
splits the fleet into two thermal populations.

cards.back:
No. The proof-of-concept benchmark sustained 2x2 HE CSI at several
hundred hertz — an order of magnitude above the paces the experiments
use.
cards.front:
Is the experiment's packet pace a hardware limit on the Pi 5 + AX210
stack?
cards.title: Capture ceiling
cards.why:
Pacing is therefore an experimental-design choice, not a ceiling. Saying
"the hardware could not go faster" would be false, and the rate ladder
later confirmed the pacer holds to 500 Hz with zero transmit errors.

cards.back:
CSI delivery is unicast by driver design: userspace registers by sending
the CSI vendor subcommand, and the driver stores that socket's portid and
targets events to it alone. Registration must come from the same netlink
socket that receives — hence a single daemon (csid) owns the stream and
fans out via a local socket.
cards.front: Why can only ONE process per node consume AX210 CSI events?
cards.title: One consumer

cards.back:
The iax backport firmware asserts (FW error in LINK_CONFIG_CMD) when the
AX210 brings up a 5 GHz AP — not a regulatory issue. Workarounds: 2.4 GHz
hostapd arms, campus-AP traffic for 5 GHz arms, or the csid injector
(monitor-mode, no AP path — works on 5 GHz).
cards.front:
What blocks 5 GHz hostapd illumination on the fleet, and what is the
workaround?
cards.title: 5 GHz AP crash

choices: Antenna count — the +30–40% gain came from joint 4-antenna 802.11ax + finer subcarrier spacing; widening 20→160 MHz alone was marginal
Bandwidth — 160 MHz resolves multipath the antennas cannot
Transmit power — SNR dominates everything
Carrier frequency — 6 GHz is strictly better
cards.explanation:
The +30–40% figure is the JOINT 4-antenna-11ax + finer-spacing move, not
antennas alone — a precision worth having exactly right when citing it.
Design consequence: sweep the antenna knob, not bandwidth, in simulation.
cards.question:
For sensing discriminability, which hardware knob matters more according
to Cominelli et al. 2023?
cards.title: Antennas vs bandwidth

cards.back:
Quasi-static night blocks separated by discrete state jumps — drift is
not a smooth ramp but plateaus punctuated by rearrangement events. First
first-party drift phenomenology; motivates event-detecting triggers over
fixed-rate assumptions.
cards.front:
What did the first 19-hour overnight ambient capture show about
environmental drift?
cards.title: Drift phenomenology

cards.back:
The competing channel fill. On the rate ladder, 250 Hz commanded against
a quiet channel delivered better than 50 Hz commanded against a busy one,
and the fleet spread widened from under a point to tens of points as the
fill rose.
cards.front:
What governs the delivered fraction of a paced probe — the commanded
rate, or something else?
cards.title: Delivery numbers
cards.why:
Two consequences. Two arms captured at different times are not comparable
on delivery, so channel fill is logged as a covariate for every analysis
window. And a rate that "failed" may only have met a busy channel.

cards.back:
A reflected copy arrives late. If the delay is comparable to the symbol
period, the echo of symbol *n* lands inside the slot of symbol *n+1* — the
receiver is decoding two symbols at once. This is **inter-symbol
interference** (ISI).

The damage is set by the RATIO of echo delay to symbol period, not by the
delay alone. Lengthen the symbol and the same room becomes harmless.

Note what this is *not*. It is not weak signal and it is not noise. Adding
transmit power makes it worse, because it amplifies the echo too.
cards.example:
Bensky's own indoor numbers (p. 291). Reflections indoors give multipath
delays "on the order of **100 ns** but may be as long as **250 ns**".

A 10 Mbit/s stream has a 100 ns bit period, so the echo covers a whole bit:
the signal "can be completely overlapped by its reflection". Hold the echo at
100 ns and stretch the symbol to the 802.11a value of 3.2 µs, and the same
reflection touches 100 / 3200 = **3.1%** of it.

Same room, same wall, same echo. Two orders of magnitude of difference in
what it costs.

figures.caption: Echo delay fixed at 100 ns throughout. Only the symbol period changes. Contaminated fraction is delay ÷ symbol period, capped at 100%.

cards.front:
A room adds echoes to a radio signal. Why does that destroy a FAST link but
not a slow one?
cards.title: Why a fast signal dies indoors
cards.why:
This is the question OFDM answers. Every design choice that follows — long
symbols, many subcarriers, the cyclic prefix — is a way of making that ratio
small.

cards.back:
It splits one fast stream across **N parallel subcarriers**, each carrying
1/N of the bits. Every lane's symbol is N times longer, and N lanes transmit
at the same instant.

Aggregate rate is unchanged. Bensky states the bookkeeping directly (p. 120):
"The symbol period is increased in each subchannel by the number of
subchannels, so the overall symbol rate doesn't change."

So the immunity is bought with **bandwidth arranged differently**, not with
throughput given up.
cards.example:
802.11a on a 20 MHz channel. 48 subcarriers carry data.

At the 54 Mbit/s rate the link moves 216 data bits per symbol. Sent
serially, each bit would occupy 4 µs / 216 ≈ **18.5 ns** — five times
shorter than the room's own echo, so unrecoverable. Sent in parallel across
48 subcarriers, each subcarrier holds its value for the full **3.2 µs**.

Identical bit rate. The echo went from fatal to negligible purely by
rearranging which bits travel together.

figures.caption: One fast lane becomes N slow lanes. The serial-to-parallel converter is where the symbol period is bought, and nothing is discarded to pay for it.

nodes.label:
fast bit stream
18.5 ns per bit

same bits per second,
173× longer symbol

cards.front:
Sending slower defeats the echo but costs throughput. What does OFDM do
instead, and why is it not just "sending slower"?
cards.title: The trade OFDM makes
cards.why:
Committees probe here to find out whether you understand OFDM as a
multiplexing scheme or have memorised "it uses an FFT".

cards.example:
802.11a, worked forwards from two chosen numbers.

The sampling rate is 20 MHz and the transform is 64 points, so
f₀ = 20 MHz / 64 = **312.5 kHz** and T = 64 / 20 MHz = **3.2 µs**. Check the
law: 1 / 3.2 µs = 312.5 kHz. It holds because it was never optional.

Now read the consequence backwards. To halve the subcarrier spacing you must
double the symbol period — which is precisely what 802.11ax does to buy
robustness in dense deployments. You cannot have narrow subcarriers and short
symbols.
cards.explanation:
Two subcarriers are **orthogonal** when the integral of their product over
one symbol period is exactly zero. Bensky (p. 292): "There will be no
interference between them if all the subcarriers are orthogonal — that is,
if the integral of any two different subcarriers over the symbol period is
zero. It is easy to show that this condition exists if the frequency
difference between adjacent subcarriers is the inverse of the symbol period."

That is the whole design, and it is a constraint rather than a tuning knob.
Choose the symbol period and the spacing is fixed. Choose the spacing and
the symbol period is fixed. There is no third choice.

The receiver's demodulator IS that integral: multiply the incoming sum by a
clean copy of the wanted subcarrier, integrate over T, and every other
subcarrier contributes zero. In practice no oscillator does this. Bensky
(pp. 121–122): "the subcarriers are created through an inverse discrete
Fourier transform, implemented as a fast Fourier transform, IFFT". The
orthogonality is a property of the transform, not of the hardware.

fields.meaning: symbol period — how long each subcarrier holds its value
spacing between adjacent subcarriers, and the lowest subcarrier frequency

figures.caption: The two quantities are one quantity. The marked crossing is 802.11a; every other OFDM system in the book sits somewhere else on the same curve.

cards.question:
Subcarriers packed side by side should interfere. State the condition that
makes them not interfere, and say what it forces.
cards.reading:
The symbol period equals the reciprocal of the spacing between adjacent
subcarriers.
cards.title: The orthogonality condition

cards.example:
Four subcarriers, all set to phase 0°, is the worst case for the power
amplifier.

At t = 0 every term equals its amplitude, so the four add coherently and the
waveform peaks at 4× the amplitude of any single subcarrier. Averaged over
the symbol the power is far lower. That gap is the **peak-to-average power
ratio**, and with 48 subcarriers rather than four it is why an OFDM amplifier
must be sized for a peak it almost never reaches.

The same picture read the other way is the payload: four QPSK subcarriers
carry 8 bits in one 3.2 µs symbol, and the messy-looking sum is those 8 bits.
cards.explanation:
Bensky Eq. 4.8, p. 122. Three things are worth reading out of it.

First, `x_k` is constant across T. Modulating a subcarrier means setting an
amplitude and a phase once, then leaving it alone — which is exactly what
makes the symbol long, and therefore what makes the echo small.

Second, the modulation order lives entirely in what values `x_k` may take.
Two bits gives four phases 90° apart, which is QPSK. Six bits gives 64
amplitude-and-phase combinations, which is 64-QAM. Nothing else in the
equation changes.

Third, the sum looks like noise on an oscilloscope and is not. It is N
independent numbers written down simultaneously, and the FFT reads them back
exactly because of the condition on the previous card.

fields.meaning: subcarrier index — which lane
the complex symbol on lane k, held CONSTANT for the whole period T
maximum amplitude of subcarrier k
subcarrier spacing, so lane k sits at frequency k·f₀
number of subcarriers

figures.caption: Four subcarriers at f₀ through 4f₀, all at phase 0°, and their sum. The sum carries every lane's symbol at once; its peak is where the peak-to-average power problem comes from.

markers.label: all four aligned — the PAPR peak

figures.x_label: time within one symbol period (fraction of T)

cards.latex: s(t) = \mathrm{Re}\left\{ \sum_{k=1}^{N} x_{k} A_{k} e^{j 2 \pi k f_{0} t} \right\}
cards.question:
Write the signal an OFDM transmitter puts on the air during one symbol, and
name what each term is doing.
cards.reading:
The transmitted waveform is the real part of a sum of N complex phasors, one
per subcarrier, each turning at an integer multiple of the base frequency.
cards.title: What is actually transmitted

cards.back:
After the IFFT, the transmitter copies the **last** slice of the symbol and
pastes it in **front**. The receiver discards that slice before the FFT.

Effect one — no ISI. Bensky (p. 125): "echoes of the previous symbol, which
are the result of multipath delays, fall in the cyclic prefix and
intersymbol interference is avoided." Everything the previous symbol
contaminated was in the part that was thrown away. This holds while the echo
delay is shorter than the prefix, and fails abruptly once it is not.

Effect two, the surprising one — echoes of the CURRENT symbol are kept, and
they **help**. Because the prefix is a copy of the symbol's own tail, a
delayed copy still presents a whole symbol inside the FFT window. Bensky:
they "will actually improve the signal-to-noise ratio". The resulting
distortion "is removed by equalization in the same manner as the flat
fading."

So a reflection stops being damage and becomes signal.
cards.example:
802.11a sizes the prefix against the room and then stops.

Prefix 0.8 µs, symbol body 3.2 µs, so 4.0 µs goes on air (p. 292). Indoor
echoes are 100–250 ns (p. 291). The margin is roughly **3× to 8×**, and it is
deliberate: "the length of the cyclic prefix is chosen to be long enough to
absorb all multipath reflections that would be expected in the environments
where the communication system is deployed."

802.11n and 802.11ac may optionally shorten it to **400 ns** (p. 295). That
is still above the 250 ns worst case, which is why it is safe indoors — and
it recovers 10% of the airtime that the 800 ns prefix was spending.

figures.caption: The prefix is a copy of the symbol's own tail. The FFT window starts after it, so the previous symbol's echo never reaches the samples that are read.

nodes.label: FFT window — what the receiver reads

cards.front:
Long symbols make the echo small. The cyclic prefix makes it zero. How, and
what is the second, less obvious thing it does?
cards.title: The cyclic prefix
cards.why:
Most people can recite that the prefix prevents ISI. The second effect is
what separates recitation from understanding, and it is the one that matters
for sensing: the receiver is not fighting multipath, it is measuring it.

choices: The previous symbol's echo now reaches past the prefix into the FFT window, so inter-symbol interference returns.
Nothing changes — the cyclic prefix is a copy of the symbol, so any delay is absorbed.
The subcarriers stop being orthogonal, because orthogonality depends on the echo delay.
The receiver loses the pilots, because pilots are transmitted inside the cyclic prefix.
cards.example:
This is the practical reason indoor and outdoor OFDM differ. 802.11a sized
its prefix for rooms with 100–250 ns spreads. Terrestrial digital video
broadcasting — also OFDM, in Bensky's own list on p. 120 — faces echoes from
hills and distant transmitters, and uses guard intervals measured in tens of
microseconds for exactly the reason this question describes.
cards.explanation:
The prefix absorbs echoes only up to its own length. At 1.2 µs the previous
symbol's tail arrives 0.4 µs after the prefix has ended, so it overlaps the
samples the FFT actually reads.

Why the others are wrong, and each is a real near-miss:

**"any delay is absorbed"** — the prefix is finite. Bensky is explicit that
its length is chosen against the *expected* deployment environment, which
means it can be exceeded by an unexpected one.

**"subcarriers stop being orthogonal"** — orthogonality is set by T = 1/f₀
alone. It is a property of the waveform, not of the room. Echo delay does not
enter that condition. What multipath does is change the channel each
subcarrier sees, which the equaliser corrects.

**"pilots are in the prefix"** — the four pilots are subcarriers, at bins
−21, −7, +7 and +21. They occupy frequency, not the prefix interval, and they
are discarded with nothing when the prefix is stripped.
cards.question:
An 802.11a link with its 0.8 µs cyclic prefix is moved into a large atrium
where the longest reflection arrives 1.2 µs after the direct path. What
actually goes wrong?
cards.title: Prefix length, tested

cards.back:
**48** carry data. **4** are pilots, at bins −21, −7, +7 and +21. **12** are
nulled: the DC bin at the centre, plus the outer bins that keep energy inside
the 20 MHz channel. That leaves 26 used bins each side of centre, and an
occupied width of 53 × 312.5 kHz = **16.5625 MHz** (p. 292).

Data rate is one division and nothing more: **data bits per symbol ÷ 4 µs**.
Two knobs set the numerator — how many bits each subcarrier carries
(1, 2, 4 or 6 for BPSK, QPSK, 16-QAM, 64-QAM) and what fraction of those are
forward-error-correction code rather than payload (1/2, 2/3 or 3/4).

The pilots are what makes the receiver's correction possible. Bensky
(p. 126): "The receiver knows what symbols are transmitted by these pilots,
so it can apply the proper correction to restore them. Through
interpellation between the pilots, it can also restore symbols on all of the
other subchannels."
cards.example:
The top rate, checked by arithmetic. 64-QAM puts 6 coded bits on each of 48
subcarriers = **288 coded bits** per symbol. At code rate 3/4 that is
288 × 3/4 = **216 data bits**. Divide by the 4 µs symbol: 216 / 4 µs =
**54 Mbit/s**.

The 72 bits of difference are the error-correcting code, and they are spread
across subcarriers by an interleaver. That is what lets a symbol survive a
subcarrier sitting in a fade (pp. 292–293): FEC "permits reconstruction of
the correct message in the receiver, even when one or more of the 48 data
channels have selective interference that would otherwise result in a lost
symbol."

figures.caption: Bensky Table 11.3, p. 293. Every row is the same division by 4 µs; only the modulation and code rate move. Coded bits per symbol is always 48 subcarriers × coded bits per subcarrier.

cards.front:
802.11a runs a 64-point transform but only 52 subcarriers are used. Account
for all 64, and say where the data rate comes from.
cards.title: The 802.11a channel, in numbers
cards.why:
Being able to derive 54 Mbit/s rather than recall it is the difference
between knowing the standard and knowing the system.

choices: Because a subcarrier at zero baseband frequency sits on the receiver's own DC offset and local-oscillator leakage, where it cannot be recovered reliably.
Because the DC bin is reserved for the cyclic prefix, which needs a subcarrier of its own.
Because an odd number of subcarriers is required for the FFT to be orthogonal.
Because the DC bin carries the pilot signal that the receiver uses to phase-lock.
cards.example:
Count the twelve unused bins to check the story holds: 1 DC bin at the
centre, plus 11 guard bins at the edges (indices beyond ±26 in a −32…+31
range). 64 − 12 = 52 used, of which 4 are pilots, leaving the 48 data
subcarriers every rate in the table is built from.
cards.explanation:
The DC bin sits at baseband zero, exactly where a direct-conversion
receiver's own DC offset and local-oscillator leakage live. Anything
transmitted there is buried under the receiver's own artefacts, so the
standard spends the bin rather than the effort. Bensky records the outcome
(p. 292): the carriers at the edges of the occupied bandwidth "and the DC
term (m = 0 …) are null".

The distractors each borrow a true fact and attach it to the wrong thing:

**"reserved for the cyclic prefix"** — the prefix is an interval of TIME
prepended to the symbol. It occupies no subcarrier at all.

**"an odd number is required"** — orthogonality follows from T = 1/f₀ and
holds for any number of subcarriers. 64 is a power of two because that is
what makes the FFT fast, not because of parity.

**"the DC bin carries the pilot"** — there are four pilots and none is at DC.
They are at bins −21, −7, +7 and +21, placed symmetrically so the receiver
can interpolate the channel across the band between them.
cards.question: Why does 802.11a leave the centre (DC) bin of its 64-point transform empty?
cards.title: Why the bins are not all used

cards.back:
A wide single carrier sees the whole reflective transfer function at once:
some frequencies reinforced, others cancelled. That is **frequency-selective
fading**, and correcting it is hard.

Narrow the lane enough and the fading across one lane is constant. That is
**flat fading**, and flat fading on one subcarrier is a single complex
number. Bensky (p. 120): OFDM "avoids frequency selective fading by
converting a high rate data stream to multiple low rate signals, which are
subjected to flat fading which can more easily be equalized and corrected by
coding and interleaving."

The fading is not removed. It is **re-indexed** into one correction per
subcarrier.

The consequence for sensing is the whole argument. To apply those
corrections the equaliser must first ESTIMATE them, once per symbol, on
every subcarrier. That vector of estimates is CSI. A sensing system adds no
sensor and no traffic — it keeps a number the receiver was already obliged
to compute and would otherwise discard.
cards.example:
Our own capture path, seen through this card. A 20 MHz HE frame on the
fleet's AX210 nodes yields a tone grid of 242 subcarriers, each a complex
number, per receive-transmit chain pair.

Nothing in that path was added for sensing. `csid` reads the channel estimate
the driver already produces from the frame preamble. That is why an
illuminated capture costs airtime and disk rather than hardware, and why the
same 802.11 receiver that decodes a frame can count the people who perturbed
it.
cards.front:
Bensky says OFDM "avoids frequency selective fading". It does not remove the
fading. What does it actually do — and what does that hand to a sensing
system?
cards.title: Flat fading, and why CSI is free
cards.why:
This is the card that connects the modulation to the thesis. If the
measurement were an extra cost, the deployment argument would collapse.

cards.back:
Bensky lists them on p. 126.

1. **Sensitivity to phase noise and Doppler.** Orthogonality assumes exact
   frequency alignment between transmitter and receiver. Any carrier offset
   leaks each subcarrier into its neighbours.
2. **High peak-to-average power ratio.** Summing many subcarriers
   occasionally aligns them all, so the amplifier must be sized for a peak it
   rarely reaches and runs inefficiently at the average.
3. **Prefix and pilots are overhead.** 0.8 µs of every 4 µs repeats
   something already sent, and 4 of 52 subcarriers carry no payload.

The first is the one that bites a sensing deployment. Transmitter and
receiver are separate unsynchronised devices, so the measured CSI carries
carrier frequency offset, sampling frequency offset and packet-detection
timing error on top of the physical channel. Communication tolerates this,
because the equaliser only needs the channel up to a common rotation.
Sensing does not, because the rotation is indistinguishable from a change in
the room until it is removed.

Against all three, Bensky calls out one advantage as the decisive one:
**scalability**. The same design widens to 40, 80 and 160 MHz with no new
modulation theory.
cards.example:
The overhead, priced exactly. The cyclic prefix is 0.8 µs of every 4.0 µs =
**20% of airtime**. The pilots are 4 of 52 occupied subcarriers = **7.7% of
the used spectrum**. Neither is recoverable, and both are the reason the
54 Mbit/s in the table is a PHY rate rather than a throughput.

The 802.11n and 802.11ac option to shorten the prefix to 400 ns cuts the
first figure from 20% to **11%**, and the fact that this is safe indoors is a
direct restatement of card 5: the room's echoes are 100–250 ns, so 400 ns
still clears them.
cards.front:
Name the three prices OFDM pays, and say which one bites hardest in a
sensing deployment.
cards.title: What OFDM costs
cards.why:
A defense question that starts "what are the limitations of…" is looking for
whether you know which limitation applies to YOUR system rather than which
ones are in the textbook.

decks.intro:
This chapter answers RQ1, and it has to survive a hostile reading of its own
title. The thesis is named after periodic BLE calibration, and the deployment
has never captured a real Bluetooth observation. That is stated plainly in the
implementation chapter and it is why this chapter's most important move is a
generalisation: BLE is one INSTANCE of a device-count channel, not the
category. Ambient device activity is a second instance, it costs no hardware,
and it is already recorded in every session the project has ever taken.
decks.title: Chapters · 6 BLE and Device-Activity Augmentation

decks.intro:
The conclusion is the chapter a committee reads twice: once at the start, to
find out what is being claimed, and once at the end, to check whether the
document delivered it. It is therefore the only chapter worth being able to
recite structurally rather than in fragments.
decks.title: Chapters · 11 Conclusion

decks.intro:
This is the chapter that reports a refutation, and it is the one a committee
will most enjoy. It builds the case for a physics prior carefully — three model
tiers, the conservation law, the closure that makes it solvable, the
physics-informed learning literature where the same construction demonstrably
works — and then kills it with a single well-designed ablation.
decks.title: Chapters · 7 Indoor Crowd Modelling

decks.intro:
This is the chapter that answers RQ2, and it is the longest for a reason: it
has to go from the physical layer to a defensible generalisation claim without
skipping the awkward middle. Four movements.
decks.title: Chapters · 5 CSI-Based Sensing

decks.intro:
The evaluation chapter was restructured on the day of this draft into three
evidence tiers, ordered by how much of the architecture each can test today.
Tier one delivers the cross-environment calibration results on public corpora.
Tier two delivers the instrument bounds. Tier three is the pre-registered
in-vivo campaign, whose protocol and thresholds are frozen and whose result
slots are labelled and empty.
decks.title: Chapters · 10 Evaluation

decks.intro:
The fusion chapter is where two heuristics turn out to be one object. The
thesis developed them separately and for different reasons: a staleness-weighted
switch that decides how much to trust an ageing anchor, and a disagreement
statistic that decides when to spend a new one. Treat the crowd count and the
slowly-drifting calibration as a latent state, and both fall out of a single
recursive Bayesian filter. Fusion is the filter's gain. The trigger is a
sequential change-point rule on its innovation.
decks.title: Chapters · 8 Calibration and Fusion

decks.intro:
Note the title. Not "Implementation" — "The Measurement Instrument". The
chapter's claim is that a synchronous multi-receiver array makes quantities
measurable that the field's methodology currently assumes, and that delivery,
loss and channel occupancy are measurands of a sensing instrument rather than
deployment plumbing.
decks.title: Chapters · 9 The Measurement Instrument

decks.intro:
The introduction has one job that the rest of the thesis depends on: it has to
make the problem sound difficult for the right reasons. Not "nobody has tried
this" — plenty have — but "every family that has tried it pays a price nobody
wants to pay." Privacy for cameras, cost for thermal, cooperation for
device-based tracking. The argument is a process of elimination that ends
somewhere specific: a passive, infrastructure-reusing, physics-grounded
modality.
decks.title: Chapters · 1 Introduction

decks.intro:
This is the chapter a committee will attack, because it is the one that makes
promises. It states, before any system is built, what the thesis intends to
answer and how it would know if it were wrong. Every hypothesis ships with an
explicit refutation condition and is maintained as a version-controlled note
revised as evidence accumulates.
decks.title: Chapters · 3 Objectives, Hypotheses and the Output Contract

decks.intro:
A literature chapter is judged on whether it organises or merely lists. This
one organises twice. It gives the CSI sensing field a four-axis taxonomy —
signal extraction, learning paradigm, deployment topology, target granularity
— and shows the axes are largely independent, so a system's position is a
combination rather than a category. Then it narrows to crowd counting and does
something braver: it tabulates the representative systems and admits the table
cannot be read as a league table, because MAE, discrete occupancy accuracy and
counting-plus-latency scores are not commensurable.
decks.title: Chapters · 2 State of the Art

decks.intro:
The design chapter has to survive a specific kind of question: not "does it
work" but "why is it shaped like that". Four tiers, mutually dependent yet
operationally separable, and the separation between the calibration regime and
the inference regime is the load-bearing part rather than an organisational
convenience.
decks.title: Chapters · 4 System Design

decks.intro:
Rewritten 2026-08-24 after a curation pass found the first version useless. It
gave the expansion, then a sentence about where the term sits in this thesis's
own architecture — which is backwards. "BLE stands for Bluetooth Low Energy,
and it is the calibration partner in the title" tells you nothing about what BLE
*is*. You cannot defend a term you can only place.
decks.title: Fundamentals · Abbreviations

decks.intro:
Rewritten 2026-08-26 after the curation pass. The first version stated each
definition correctly and then stopped. Four notes said the same thing four
ways — redefine in human words, show the algebra, give sample values, provide
plots — and the shortest summary of all of them is that a symbol you have
only ever seen in a sentence is a symbol you cannot use.
decks.title: Fundamentals · Definitions and symbols

decks.intro:
In July 2026 the thesis was read cold and the verdict was uncomfortable: a
competent measurement study with childish mathematics. Numbers everywhere, no
theory holding them. The four pillars were the answer, and this deck is what
the pillars reduce to — the dozen equations that carry the whole apparatus.
decks.title: Fundamentals · The formulas

decks.intro:
A defense rehearsal that drills a paraphrase of a research question is worse
than one that drills nothing, because it teaches you to answer a question the
document does not ask. So these cards are not written — they are rendered from
the same declaration the thesis itself renders from. If a question changes in
`Foundation.md`, it changes here, and nowhere is there a second copy to drift.
decks.title: Fundamentals · The research questions

decks.intro:
The commonest defense failure is not a wrong answer. It is a right answer given
from the wrong chapter — reaching for the evaluation numbers when the question
was about the architecture, or defending the instrument when the question was
about the corpus. A committee reads that as a document you have written rather
than a document you have organised.
decks.title: Fundamentals · Topics: what lives where

decks.intro:
Watch people leave a lecture hall and you will see physics: flow through the
door saturates, a queue crystallises, walking speed collapses as density
rises. Pedestrian dynamics is the discipline that made those observations
quantitative — measured on real crowds, in units of persons per square metre
— and it matters here for a simple reason: our synthetic CSI experiments are
only as credible as the crowds that generate them. If the simulated people
move wrongly, every downstream channel measurement inherits the lie. So this
track is about the walking layer: the models, the handful of parameters that
are actually grounded in literature, and the discipline of not tuning them
until an experiment happens to pass.
decks.title: CRD503 · Crowd dynamics and pedestrian simulation

decks.intro:
Committees are not adversaries; they are professionals with forty minutes to
decide whether you own your work. Their big questions are predictable in
form — summarise it, defend its worth, name its weakness, tell us what is
genuinely new — and unpredictable only in phrasing. The winning shape for an
answer is nearly always the same: concede what must be conceded in the first
sentence, then show that the concession was already priced in. "The biggest
threat is X, which is why the design includes Y" reads as command; a
defensive "well, actually" reads as fragility. The model answers here are
not scripts to memorise. Read them for their skeletons — claim, evidence,
honest limit, next step — then practise saying each one in your own words,
shorter every time.
decks.title: Defense · The big committee questions

decks.intro:
The most dangerous errors in a defense are the ones you brought yourself: a
number quoted from memory of a summary of a paper, drifted three retellings
from the source. We know exactly what these look like because a 2026 audit
of our own vault caught several — a decay figure attributed to the wrong
paper and the wrong metric, our own re-analysis numbers credited to the
dataset's authors, a formula cited to papers that never derived it. All were
fixed at source; here they are preserved deliberately, as sparring partners.
Each question below offers the seductive wrong version alongside the
audited truth. If you can feel WHY the wrong option is tempting, you are
inoculated; if you merely know the right answer, the temptation returns
under pressure.
decks.title: Defense · Committee traps and near-miss claims

decks.intro:
Formal methods have a reputation for living far from real systems, but in
this project they do manual labour. State machines drive every simulated
occupant's day; typed schemas reject malformed experiments before a single
CPU-hour is burned; a Petri net models a message pipeline in the Hermod
paper. The through-line of this short track is that a formal model is a
contract you can be held to — it makes wrong states unrepresentable and
wrong claims checkable. That mindset, more than any particular logic, is
what transfers: the same instinct that adds a timeout guard to a looping
state machine also adds a defeater clause to a hypothesis.
decks.title: FM505 · Formal modelling and verification

decks.intro:
Right now your phone is shouting into the void several times a second. BLE
advertisements — tiny broadcast packets on three channels wedged between
Wi-Fi's territory — power everything from AirTags to COVID exposure apps,
and they leak a physical quantity for free: received signal strength. It is
a crude quantity, single-number, fading-battered. But crude, cheap, and
everywhere beats precise, expensive, and absent — which is exactly the role
BLE plays in this thesis. Not the star sensor, but the honest witness: the
side-channel that tells a drifting CSI model what the ground truth roughly
is, and does so with radios the building already owns.
decks.title: LOC502 · BLE and RF localization

decks.intro:
If the defense has a home turf for the committee, it is statistics. Nobody
will re-derive your ray tracer on a whiteboard, but anyone can ask what your
confidence interval means or why you trusted a p-value at n=3. This track
collects the methods the thesis actually leans on — not statistics in
general, but the specific tools wired into the campaign reductions, each
with the scar that taught us to use it: the pilot correlation that shrank
under replication, the dataset that scored perfectly for the wrong reason,
the significant p-value that arrived exactly when the effect got smaller.
The theme throughout: effect sizes with intervals over verdicts, named
baselines over naked numbers, and pre-registration over hindsight.
decks.title: PRB504 · Probabilistic and statistical methods

decks.intro:
Why simulate at all? Because some experiments are unaffordable, unethical, or
simply impossible: you cannot rearrange a building's walls fifty times, or
hire thirty people to walk identical evenings for twenty random seeds. A
ray-traced radio channel coupled to a simulated crowd buys those experiments
for the price of CPU time. The danger is equally plain — a simulator is a
theory wearing an execution engine, and it will happily confirm the
assumptions you fed it. So this track carries both halves: the machinery
(what the toolchain actually computes) and the epistemics (which claims
survived contact with real data, which failed, and what each failure taught
us about the machine).
decks.title: SIM507 · Simulation toolkits and sim-to-real discipline

decks.intro:
In July 2026 the thesis changed shape. Reading the progress deck cold, the
verdict was uncomfortable: a competent measurement study with childish
mathematics — numbers everywhere, no theory holding them. The response was
not to measure more but to ask what single formal structure would make the
existing results inevitable. The answer became four pillars: a hierarchical
calibration model, a derived scattering law, a state-space view of fusion,
and a spectral-plus-coverage layer. Each pillar takes results that were
already in hand and re-derives them as predictions — the difference between
"we observed 42% recovery" and "the model says two anchors must recover
about this much, and they do." This deck is that theoretical core, pillar by
pillar, with its evidence and its honest gaps.
decks.title: Thesis · The four-pillar theoretical core

decks.intro:
A thesis is usually presented as a single claim. Managed honestly, it is a
portfolio of bets at different odds — and this one keeps the ledger in the
open: twenty living hypotheses, each with a machine-readable state, a
confidence score, a novelty score against named prior art, and a
pre-declared gate that would promote or kill it. The portfolio view changes
how you defend. You stop protecting weak claims (the ledger already marks
them plausible, not proven) and you stop underselling strong ones. And when
a committee member finds the refuted entries, they find evidence of a
falsification machine that actually fires — which is worth more than another
confirmation. These cards walk the bets that matter, from the anchor premise
to the flagship gamble.
decks.title: Thesis · The living-hypothesis portfolio

decks.intro:
Between the physics and the science sits a layer nobody thanks you for:
getting honest bits out of commodity silicon. Wi-Fi chips were never meant to
export their channel estimates, so every CSI dataset in the literature rests
on some half-documented vendor path — and on the assumption that the bytes
mean what the README says. Our fleet taught us how dangerous that assumption
is: two silent data-corruption bugs sat in the capture stack, invisible in
amplitude plots, poisoning every phase analysis. This deck is the
instrument-builder's view of the thesis — what the hardware actually does,
which numbers you measured yourself, and why "verify your own pipeline"
became a design principle rather than a slogan.
decks.title: WS501 · CSI extraction, hardware, and the AX210 fleet

decks.intro:

decks.title: WS501 · OFDM from zero

decks.intro:
Every Wi-Fi router is an unpaid physicist. Twenty times a second it solves a
scattering problem — how did the room transform my signal? — because it must,
to decode the next frame. For thirty years that answer was computed, used, and
thrown away. This track is about keeping it. The channel estimate a router
discards is a measurement of the space between antennas: the walls, the
furniture, and crucially the people. Before any claim about counting crowds
can make sense, you need to feel why a room full of people IS a different
radio channel than an empty one. That is what these first cards build, from
the physics up.
